title: Bottleneck Width, Loss Design and the Limits of Skip-Free Convolutional Denoising Autoencoders for Simulated Low-Dose CT
abstract: Abstract Convolutional denoising autoencoders (DAEs) are attractive for computed tomography (CT) because they offer a small model and a compact, reusable latent code, but it is unclear whether a skip-free DAE can compete with feed-forward residual networks. We examine this question on 41 abdominal CT volumes from the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (820 real slices, split by volume) and 300 synthetic multi-material phantoms, corrupted with a two-stage noise model (Poisson photon noise followed by Gaussian read noise). We train convolutional DAEs with bottleneck widths of 8 to 256 channels, a variational variant and a composite MSE+SSIM loss, and compare them with a DnCNN-style network and with Gaussian, median and non-local-means filters on identical held-out volumes. DnCNN reached 44.21 dB PSNR and 0.979 SSIM, against 35.07 dB and 0.938 for the best MSE-trained autoencoder; the noisy input scored 35.56 dB and 0.756. The composite loss raised the autoencoder to 35.65 dB and 0.950. Quality was flat between 32 and 256 channels (PSNR spread 0.22 dB) and dropped only at 16 and 8 channels (− 0.9 and − 2.5 dB relative to width 128). On real slices the width-128 autoencoder lowered PSNR relative to the noisy input in 71% of cases, mainly at thin, high-contrast structures, even though SSIM improved by about 0.12. Latent codes predicted phantom material with 66–84% accuracy (chance 20%) but formed no clusters (silhouette ≈ 0). The autoencoder needed about 34 times less compute per tile than DnCNN, yet was far less accurate. In this setting the reconstruction-through-a-bottleneck design, rather than bottleneck size, appears to limit denoising quality; the role of skip connections remains to be isolated.

title: Shape and Attenuation Cues for Defect-Type Classification in X‑ray CT: A Controlled Synthetic Study with a 3D CNN
abstract: Abstract After a candidate defect has been located in an X-ray computed tomography (CT) volume, an inspector must still decide whether it is a pore, a crack or an inclusion, because each type has different acceptance criteria and root causes. Pores and cracks are voids with near-zero attenuation, whereas inclusions have a distinct, non-zero attenuation, so intensity should help where shape alone is ambiguous. We test this in a controlled synthetic study: 7,500 exactly labelled 3D patches (2,500 per class) generated from 200 simulated scans with partial-volume blur, shading and Poisson–Gaussian noise at three SNR levels, split by scan into training, validation and test sets. A compact 3D CNN (0.88 M parameters) reaches 0.990 test accuracy (0.990 ± 0.002 over five training seeds; 95% CI of the headline run 0.984–0.996). An identical network given only binary masks reaches 0.824 ± 0.015, a drop of 16.6 ± 1.6 points. In the headline run (drop 17.5 points; McNemar exact p ≈ 10⁻⁵⁰) the loss is confined to pore–inclusion confusion, cracks being recognised perfectly, and comes almost entirely from spherical inclusions, whose masks resemble spherical pores. Random Forest and SVM classifiers on shape and intensity features perform similarly (0.988–0.997), so the CNN is competitive rather than superior. All 11 errors of the headline run are either dark inclusions with contrast close to that of a void or pores and cracks of 59–69 voxels, and accuracy did not degrade from SNR 40 to 10. Because the data are synthetic, the results are an upper bound for real scans.

title: Non-invasive Prediction of Molecular and Histopathological Subtypes in Murine and Human Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Using [18F]FDG PET
abstract: Abstract Purpose This study evaluates the utility of [ 18 F]fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography ([ 18 F]FDG PET) for Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) subtype differentiation across preclinical and clinical settings, and assesses the impact of tracer uptake timing on subtype discrimination. Methods [ 18 F]FDG uptake was investigated in classical (C)-HPAC and quasi-mesenchymal (QM)-PSN1 cells, heterotopic rat (n = 11), orthotopic mouse xenografts (n = 8), and gland-forming (GF)/non-GF tumors from seven genetically engineered mouse models (GEMMs). Retrospective [ 18 F]FDG PET data from 16 PDAC patients were analyzed using subtype classification based on keratin-81 (KRT81+(QM)/KRT81-(non-QM)). Dynamic and static [ 18 F]FDG PET parameters, including standard uptake value (SUV) mean , SUV max , and mean tumor-to-muscle ratio (T/M mean ), were evaluated for subtype discrimination. Results QM tumors showed significantly higher [ 18 F]FDG uptake than C tumors in vitro (50.7 ± 1.03% vs. 19.4 ± 2.37%), in heterotopic (SUV max 6.91 ± 1.14 vs. 2.66 ± 0.28), and orthotopic (SUV max 2.85 ± 0.70 vs. 1.45 ± 0.50) xenografts. Non-GF tumors also showed significantly higher uptake than GF (SUV max 3.94 ± 0.70 vs. 2.53 ± 0.97). Patients showed a similar trend (SUV max 6.33 ± 1.74 vs. 4.95 ± 1.46), with shorter overall survival in QM tumors. Dynamic PET revealed continued tracer accumulation in QM/non-GF tumors throughout the 90-minute acquisition period, whereas C/GF tumors approached a plateau by approximately 60 minutes. T/M mean showed the best classification performance across all models. Conclusion [ 18 F]FDG PET differentiated PDAC subtypes across all preclinical models with a similar but less pronounced trend in patients. Later imaging time points showed enhanced metabolic separation, suggesting potential benefits for improving non-invasive subtype discrimination. Clinical Trial Registration N/A

title: AI-Based 3D Pore Volume and Morphology Prediction
abstract: Abstract X-ray computed tomography can quantify pores inside a material, but noisy and blurred pore boundaries make measurements sensitive to the segmentation procedure. This work evaluates direct regression of pore volume, surface area proxy, sphericity, and elongation from a centered synthetic grayscale crop. We generated 180 independent sphere, ellipsoid, and irregular pore geometries and rendered each under three degradation conditions, yielding 540 crops of size 24 3 . All renderings of each geometry remained in one split. A compact three-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN) was compared with Otsu thresholding and an Extra Trees regressor using segmentation and intensity features. On 27 held-out geometries at high degradation, volume mean absolute percentage error was 14.76% for the CNN, 67.29% for Otsu, and 3.74% for Extra Trees. Otsu recovered clean discrete volume exactly and had the lowest pooled elongation error. Paired and out-of-domain experiments reveal how size, nearby pores, unresolved features, and sampling affect the results. The contribution is a reproducible synthetic benchmark that identifies conditions under which learned estimation improves on thresholding and conditions where classical measurements remain stronger. Independent industrial scans are needed to assess transfer.

title: AI-Based Prediction of Total Porosity Volume Fraction from 3D CT Volumes: A Volumetric Regression Approach
abstract: Abstract Computed Tomography (CT) is a premier non-destructive testing (NDT) modality used for inspecting internal defects, particularly porosity in additive manufacturing and metal castings. The standard industry workflow relies on voxel-wise image segmentation (e.g., Otsu thresholding) to separate void spaces from the solid matrix before calculating the total Porosity Volume Fraction (PVF). However, this segmentation step is highly brittle under severe measurement noise and artifacts, leading to catastrophic miscalculations. In this paper, we propose a direct deep-learning regression approach using a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) equipped with Global Average Pooling (GAP) to predict scalar PVF directly from noisy 3D CT volumes, bypassing segmentation entirely. To validate this hypothesis, we engineered a rigorous synthetic 3D CT dataset containing 500 procedural phantoms with precisely controlled spherical pores and uniformly distributed PVF ranging from 0.1% to 15%. We degraded these volumes with varying levels of Gaussian noise (10 dB, 20 dB, and 30 dB SNR). The 3D CNN was evaluated against classical Otsu thresholding and a Random Forest (RF) machine learning baseline utilizing global intensity statistics. Our results demonstrate that the 3D CNN is exceptionally robust, maintaining a low Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.363 percentage points even under extreme 10 dB noise, where Otsu thresholding catastrophically collapses (MAE of 11.51 pp). Unexpectedly, the RF baseline achieved the lowest overall MAE (0.088 pp). Through a rigorous evidence audit and domain-shift experiment involving a simulated beam-hardening cupping artifact, we dissect this phenomenon, revealing that the RF's superiority is a statistical artifact of the synthetic data's homogenous matrix assumption. This research highlights the viability of segmentation-free volumetric regression for NDT while providing a critical warning regarding 'shortcut learning' in synthetic physics datasets.

title: Sparse-View CT Reconstruction Using Deep Learning
abstract: Abstract Sparse-view computed tomography (CT) reduces radiation dose and scan time by acquiring few projection angles but filtered back-projection (FBP) of such data suffers from severe streak artefacts because the angular sampling falls far below the Nyquist requirement. We study the post-processing approach in which a residual U-Net removes these artefacts from the FBP image, and test it on five synthetic datasets that differ in object class and physics: head phantoms at normal dose, chest phantoms at ten-fold lower dose, aluminium machined parts, photon-starved titanium components, and aluminium resolution targets. Sinograms at 30, 60 and 90 views are simulated with the Beer-Lambert law, Poisson photon statistics and Gaussian read noise, and the network is compared against FBP and the Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (SART), both with settings tuned on validation data. On 150 held-out test images per dataset, the U-Net achieves the highest peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) in all 15 dataset and view settings, improving on the best classical method by 1.9 to 5.8 dB (paired Wilcoxon test, p < 10⁻²⁰ in every setting), and at 30 views it exceeds the PSNR of 180-view FBP on all five datasets, while running in about 20 ms per image on a CPU. Stress tests show the limits of the approach: networks transfer between similar industrial datasets but degrade or harm images of other object classes, fail when the test data are more sparsely sampled or receive ten times fewer photons than in training, and are outperformed by SART on the unseen Shepp-Logan phantom. A network trained on resolution targets does generalise to a resolution plate taken from laboratory data, improving on SART by 2.7 to 3.4 dB. The code, data and trained models are released for full reproducibility.

title: Deep Learning Ring Artifact Removal in Computed Tomography: A Two-Head U-Net Benchmarked Against Classical Radial profile Filtering
abstract: Abstract Ring artifacts, caused by detector pixels whose gain or offset is slightly wrong, appear in reconstructed computed tomography (CT) slices as concentric circles around the rotation centre. They can hide small features and break threshold-based segmentation. Classical ring removal relies on hand-tuned filters, and real scans have no ground truth for measuring how well a method works. This project builds a synthetic CT pipeline (phantom, parallel-beam projection, Poisson noise, detector gain and offset error, filtered back-projection) in which the true ring is known for every image, and trains a two-head U-Net that predicts the ring image, which is subtracted from the input, and a ring mask. On 1000 training, 100 validation and 100 test slices of 256 × 256 pixels, where the test slices come from a phantom family never seen in training, the U-Net raises the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) from 33.11 dB to 39.54 dB and the structural similarity (SSIM) from 0.868 to 0.957. A radial-profile classical baseline tuned on the validation set gains 0.77 dB on validation but loses 0.56 dB on the unseen family. The U-Net gain depends on ring type, from +13.9 dB for dead_hot rings to +0.4 dB for faint band rings. Training with 100, 500 and 1000 images gives 35.29, 38.42 and 39.54 dB; three random seeds give 39.40 ± 0.15 dB; removing the Dice term from the loss raises PSNR to 39.89 dB but lowers mask Dice from 0.640 to 0.605. The mask head is the weaker output (Dice 0.640 overall, 0.07 on band rings). Because all data are simulated, the sim-to-real gap remains the main open question.

The U-Net gain depends on ring type, from +13.9 dB for dead_hot rings to +0.4 dB for faint band rings. Training with 100, 500 and 1000 images gives 35.29, 38.42 and 39.54 dB; three random seeds give 39.40 ± 0.15 dB; removing the Dice term from the loss raises PSNR to 39.89 dB but lowers mask Dice from 0.640 to 0.605. The mask head is the weaker output (Dice 0.640 overall, 0.07 on band rings). Because all data are simulated, the sim-to-real gap remains the main open question.

title: Controlled Benchmarking and Robustness Analysis of Classical Machine-Learning Approaches for Synthetic CT Sample Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Reliable delineation of a specimen from its surrounding background is a prerequisite for quantitative analysis of computed tomography (CT) images. This work is positioned as a controlled benchmarking and robustness study of classical machine-learning approaches for binary sample–background segmentation in synthetic CT-like images, rather than as a demonstration of validated industrial CT applicability. Five supervised classifiers—Logistic Regression (LR), Gaussian Naive Bayes (GNB), linear Support Vector Machine (SVM), Decision Tree (DT), and Random Forest (RF)—are compared using a synthetic dataset of 300 grayscale images (256 × 256 pixels) with corresponding binary reference masks. Three pixel-level feature representations are examined: intensity alone; intensity with normalized spatial coordinates; and a five-dimensional representation comprising intensity, two spatial coordinates, local mean, and local standard deviation calculated over a 5 × 5 neighbourhood. The dataset is divided into training, validation, and testing subsets containing 210, 45, and 45 images, respectively. Under the constructed synthetic conditions, the DT classifier using the complete feature set achieves the highest reported mean test accuracy (0.9998), Dice coefficient (0.9997), and intersection over union (IoU; 0.9995). Sensitivity experiments reveal marked performance degradation as additive Gaussian noise increases and image contrast decreases, whereas increasing the training-set size produces only marginal gains. The principal contribution is a controlled comparison of classical pixel-wise classifiers, an assessment of feature-engineering effects, and a robustness analysis under specified synthetic perturbations. The results characterize model behaviour within the defined synthetic data-generating process; they do not establish performance on experimental or industrial XCT data. Validation using independent, representative XCT scans is a necessary subsequent step.

title: Deterministic and Gaussian Decoder LoRA for Point-Prompted Abdominal CT Segmentation
abstract: Abstract This study examines deterministic low-rank adaptation (LoRA) and Gaussian decoder LoRA with heuristic rank selection for point-prompted abdominal CT segmentation using SAM2. Both approaches were evaluated on a single BTCV split comprising 19 training, five validation, and six test volumes, with one training seed and 2,466 matched positive-point prompts. Across 78 volume–organ pairs, mean Dice scores were 0.5123 for frozen SAM2, 0.8049 for deterministic LoRA, and 0.7982 for Gaussian decoder LoRA. The deterministic model achieved a 0.667-percentage-point advantage under equal volume– organ weighting (descriptive 95% t interval: −0.214 to +1.549), although the difference became −0.019 points under equal prompt weighting. We also investigated whether decoder uncertainty provides additional information for identifying segmentation failures. Adding full-image mutual information (MI) to a failureranking model containing organ identity, predicted area, and entropy produced a negligible change in mean AUROC (−0.0001). Retrospective inference-only analyses showed similarly limited effects from replacing learned decoder standard deviations with fixed values. Adding dropout MI to organ, area, and entropy on 189 deterministic-model failures changed AUROC from 0.8222 to 0.8238. The Gaussian decoder also required substantially more inference time than its deterministic counterpart. Both adaptation strategies improved overlap relative to frozen SAM2, but the available evidence does not establish a consistent advantage for Gaussian decoder adaptation or its uncertainty estimates beyond simpler alternatives.

title: Neuroimaging Cranial Pathology Delineation through Contrast-Specialized Specialist Routing
abstract: Abstract Purpose Cranial MRI reaches the reading room in whatever contrast combination the scanner, site and protocol produced, and lesion appearance changes with contrast. A department that wants segmentation support must maintain a separate model for each contrast combination, a library that is hard to sustain in routine practice. We evaluated a single deep learning framework that replaces that library with contrast-specialised routing. Materials and methods The framework (OMNIA) keeps one specialist subnetwork for each MR contrast and fuses their predictions at every resolution level through a hierarchical gating network that assigns voxelwise weights. Progressive training protects each specialist's contrast-specific behaviour, and a soft allocation module routes incomplete contrast sets to the specialist channels under an availability prior. The study was retrospective, across nine collections totalling 6,336 annotated volumes, five contrasts and six pathology groups, with a healthy reference collection; six public collections were used for training and internal testing, and three institutional collections were held back for external testing. Results On the seen collections the framework reached a mean Dice of 0.8204, above every universal baseline (0.8007–0.8084) and close to dedicated per-combination pipelines (0.8250), as a single deployable model. On the unseen collections it reached 0.7951, the strongest result among single models. On multi-contrast BraTS 2021 input it scored 0.8334 against 0.8366 for fifteen dedicated models, at about one third of their storage (1.65 GB versus about 4.95 GB). Conclusion Contrast-specialised routing allows one deployable model to approach the accuracy of dedicated per-combination pipelines, on data and contrast combinations beyond those it was trained on.

title: Measuring lesion–vascular context for diabetic retinopathy grading and retinal phenotyping
abstract: Abstract BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) grades summarise severity but do not quantify the vascular surroundings of individual lesions. We investigated whether measured lesion–vascular context improves lesion-based grading and characterises vascular variation beyond severity. SUBJECTS/METHODS: This cross-sectional secondary analysis of public datasets matched 2,874 APTOS photographs to lesion predictions and AutoMorph vascular measurements (1,724 training, 575 validation, 575 test). Five models trained exclusively on DDR annotations predicted four lesion families. Registered anatomy yielded 24 spatial descriptors and 1,584 lesion–biomarker products. Structured ordinal models, an anatomical graph and six frozen image encoders evaluated grading. Separate grade-adjusted analyses assessed vascular associations and prediction. RESULTS: Structured context increased test quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) from 0.764 to 0.827 (difference 0.063; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.028–0.099). The graph achieved QWK 0.849 and macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.924 (QWK difference 0.085; 95% CI 0.050–0.119); both comparisons with lesion-only grading had false-discovery-rate-adjusted 𝑞 < 0.001. Individual contextual additions were not separately supported. Graph sensitivity for proliferative DR was 0.316, compared with 0.605 for structured context. Grade-adjusted analysis supported 103 lesion–biomarker associations, and lesion counts improved prediction of 26/66 vascular measurements, predominantly calibre/width and fractal measures. CONCLUSIONS: Combined lesion–vascular representations improved lesion-only grading and characterised vascular variation within severity categories. The measurements provide inspectable anatomical evidence, but segmentation limitations and classwise errors preclude claims of clinical readiness or prognostic validity.

title: Deterministic projection selection for Limited-View Computed Tomography
abstract: Abstract In Limited-View Computed Tomography (LVCT), one restricts the number of projection angles (or views) for data reduction, which has many implications, especially in medical domain. In most of the existing works on LVCT, the views are sampled randomly or in equi-spaced manner, which makes the sampling process oblivion to the image reconstruction solvers. Motivated by this gap between the sampling strategy and the image reconstruction solvers, we propose a deterministic way of finding an optimal set of views for LVCT using block-sparse optimization problem. The proposed methodology is tied to a selection of Radon sub-matrix possessing low total coherence which is desired for sparsity-based CT image reconstruction. We demonstrate efficacy of the proposed deterministic LVCT in recovering CT images.

title: A Comparative Study of Lightweight Uncertainty-Aware Bayesian CNNs and Ensemble Models for MRI-Based ASD Diagnosis
abstract: Abstract Background: Early and accurate diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is essential for improving clinical outcomes. Although deep learning (DL) has demonstrated strong potential in analyzing structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (sMRI), most existing frameworks rely on deterministic models that lack uncertainty quantification—an essential component for clinical decision-making—and often involve high computational complexity, limiting real-world applicability. Objective: This study aims to conduct a comprehensive comparative evaluation of three deep learning paradigms to develop a robust and uncertainty-aware framework for ASD diagnosis using multi-orientational MRI data (axial, coronal, and sagittal views). Methods: We systematically evaluated three categories of models: (1) fine-tuned deterministic architectures, including EfficientNetV2B0, EfficientNetB3, and MobileNetV2; (2) ensemble learning strategies, including averaging, majority voting, weighted averaging, and stacked generalization; and (3) lightweight Bayesian convolutional neural networks (CNNs) incorporating Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout and Variational Inference (VI) to estimate predictive uncertainty. This hierarchical framework enables a balanced assessment of diagnostic accuracy and model reliability. Results: Experimental results demonstrate that ensemble models achieved the highest classification performance, with a peak accuracy of 99.51% in the coronal view. Notably, the proposed lightweight Bayesian CNNs delivered competitive performance while providing well-calibrated uncertainty estimates, enabling the identification of ambiguous and out-of-distribution cases. Additionally, Grad-CAM visualizations revealed that model attention is concentrated in clinically relevant regions, particularly the frontal and temporal lobes, supporting the neurobiological plausibility of the predictions. Conclusion: This study highlights that integrating uncertainty quantification into lightweight deep learning architectures enhances both transparency and reliability compared to conventional deterministic approaches.

title: Prompt-Conditioned Channel Attention for Hierarchical Feature Modulation toward Anatomy-Agnostic Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Accurate and anatomically plausible medical image segmentation remains challenging due to low contrast, ambiguous boundaries, interpatient variability, and modality-specific artifacts. Interactive segmentation using spatial prompts has emerged as a promising strategyto guide attention and improve localization, particularly in low-contrast or structurally ambiguous regions. However, existing methodstypically restrict prompt integration to late-stage fusion and lack explicit mechanisms for channel-wise feature modulation, limiting theirability to capture deeper contextual and modality-specific variations across hierarchical representations. To address these limitations, weintroduce Prompt-Conditioned Channel Attention (PCCA), a novel modulation mechanism that enables deep, hierarchical integration ofsemantic prompts within encoder-decoder segmentation networks. PCCA extracts compact channel descriptors from both image and promptfeatures via pooling, projects them into a shared latent space, and fuses them through a gated excitation unit to compute prompt-awarechannel attention weights. These weights perform hierarchical channel-wise attention by adaptively reweighting feature responses atevery network stage, enabling spatially selective and semantically enriched representations. Building on this mechanism, we proposePROMISE-Net (PROmpt Modulated Integration for SEgmentation), instantiated in two architectural variants: a convolutional model(PROMISE-CNN) and a transformer-based model (PROMISE-Txformer). Across ISIC-Lesion, Kvasir-Polyp, CAMUS-Cardiac, andKvasir-Instrument benchmarks, integrating PCCA into PROMISE-CNN yielded relative IoU improvements of 10.4%, 8.7%, 0.8%, and3.4% over baseline U-Net, while PROMISE-Txformer achieved corresponding gains of 7.6%, 23%, 2.1%, and 1.1% over baseline UNETR.These results demonstrate consistent cross-architectural, cross-modal, and cross-anatomical improvements, establishing PCCA coupledPROMISE-Net as a scalable and generalizable framework for prompt-aware feature modulation in medical image segmentation. The codeis available at https://github.com/kamruleee51/PROMISENet.

title: Diagnostic yield of CT angiography for pulmonary embolism in patients with interstitial lung disease admitted for acute respiratory worsening
abstract: Abstract Introduction : Acute respiratory worsening (ARW) in interstitial lung disease (ILD) is a critical clinical event with a broad differential diagnosis. Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a potential trigger, but its frequency, predictors, and prognostic implications in this setting remain poorly defined. Objective : To evaluate the diagnostic yield of CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) for PE, associated clinical features, and outcomes in patients with ILD admitted with ARW. Methods : This retrospective cohort study analyzed ILD patients admitted to a tertiary center (2017–2023) for ARW who underwent CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) within 72 hours. Data were retrieved using the MDClone platform and individual chart review, including demographic, clinical, and laboratory variables. In an exploratory analysis, CTPA results were compared with those of non-ILD patients who underwent CTPA, matched for age, sex, and smoking status. Results : Of 2,564 ILD admissions 439 were due to ARW, and CTPA was performed in 77 (17.5%, 68 unique patients). PE was diagnosed in 14 of these admissions (18.2% diagnostic yield). Individual clinical and laboratory features (tachycardia, hypoxemia, D-dimer, malignancy, and clinical signs of deep vein thrombosis) did not differ significantly between PE-positive and PE-negative admissions, with the exception of smoking status: PE was more frequent among never-smokers compared to current or former smokers (31.3% vs. 9.1%; OR 4.55; 95% CI 1.3–16.2), an association that persisted at the patient level and after adjustment for ILD type and age. At the patient level, the proportion of positive examinations was higher compared to matched controls (20.6% vs. 11.0%, p=0.04). No statistically significant association between PE and short- or long-term survival was detected. Conclusion : Among ILD patients with ARW who were selected for CTPA, approximately one in five had PE. Individual clinical and laboratory features did not reliably distinguish patients with PE, and the association with never-smoking status warrants confirmation. Prospective studies are needed to define the optimal diagnostic strategy for PE in this population.

title: CGMU-Net: A Classification-Guided Cross-Interaction Network for Computer-Assisted Dermoscopy Skin Lesion Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Accurate and effective segmentation of dermoscopic skin lesions is critical for clinical diagnosis. Despite recent advances in deep learning, challenges such as irregular shapes, blurred boundaries, and low contrast remain. To address these issues, we propose CGMU-Net, a classification-guided cross-interaction network. The model integrates a cross-interaction attention fusion module to enhance semantic--boundary feature interaction, a channel-wise feature enhancement module to improve multi-scale consistency, and a classification-guided lesion-aware module to introduce discriminative cues. Experimental results on three public datasets (ISIC 2017, ISIC 2018, and PH2) demonstrate that CGMU-Net achieves Dice scores of 89.21%, 89.91%, and 95.01%, respectively. These results indicate that the proposed method provides accurate and robust lesion segmentation.

title: Ultrasound-Guided Pudendal Nerve Block in Elderly Pelvic Organ Prolapse Surgery: Impact on Anesthetic Consumption and Postoperative Recovery-A Randomized Clinical Trial.
abstract: Background Nerve block is often used for multimodal analgesia. Surgeries for pelvic organ prolapse (POP) in elderly patients are focused on the perineal area, where pudendal nerve block (PNB) can provide analgesia or anaesthesia. There are limited studies on PNB in POP surgery, mainly addressing postoperative pain relief. This prospective randomized controlled trial examined the impact of ultrasound-guided PNB on intraoperative medication and postoperative recovery in elderly POP surgery patients. Methods Patients aged 60-70 undergoing total vaginal hysterectomy (with or without sacral fixation/colporrhaphy) under general anesthesia were randomized into two groups: PNB (pudendal nerve block) and NPNB (no pudendal nerve block). Anesthesia was induced with target-controlled infusions of remifentanil (3 ng/mL) and propofol (3 µg/mL). The study compared intraoperative anesthetic doses, hemodynamic changes, cardiovascular drug needs, wakefulness time, and post-op recovery quality between the groups. Results 58 patients completed the study. The PNB group required significantly less remifentanil (386.6 ± 239.1 µg vs 563.1 ± 235.7 µg, p = 0.005) and propofol (645.5 ± 315.2 mg vs 804.2 ± 297.2 mg, p = 0.028) compared to the NPNB group. Intraoperative hemodynamics were more stable in the PNB group, with a reduced need for vasopressors. The PNB group also exhibited faster emergence, lower postoperative pain, and less oversedation,with a non-significant trend toward higher QoR-40 scores. Conclusions Ultrasound-guided PNB in elderly POP surgery patients reduced opioid and anesthetic doses, shortened awakening time, and produced clinically favourable improvements in postoperative recovery. Larger studies are needed to confirm these benefits for postoperative rehabilitation.

title: Successful Trastuzumab Desensitization After a Severe Infusion-Related Reaction with Acute Hypoxemia and Suspected Pulmonary Toxicity in HER2-Positive Metastatic Breast Cancer: A Case Report.
abstract: Trastuzumab is a cornerstone of treatment for HER2-positive breast cancer. Infusion-related reactions are common during the first administration, but severe reactions with hemodynamic instability and acute respiratory compromise are uncommon. We report a 36-year-old woman with de novo HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer involving the lungs who developed hypotension, presyncope, oxygen desaturation, and acute hypoxemic respiratory failure 35 minutes after the initiation of her first trastuzumab infusion. Chest computed tomography showed known bilateral pulmonary metastases and new bibasal opacities, raising concern for an overlapping severe infusion-related reaction and inflammatory pulmonary toxicity. Trastuzumab was discontinued, and the patient recovered after respiratory support and systemic corticosteroids. Following complete clinical recovery and resolution of the inflammatory radiological findings, a multidisciplinary team performed a rapid drug desensitization protocol under intensive care monitoring. The full trastuzumab target dose was successfully administered without immediate or delayed breakthrough reaction, and the protocol was repeated in subsequent 12 total cycles, allowing continued HER2-targeted therapy without disease progression. This case illustrates that rapid drug desensitization may permit trastuzumab reintroduction after a severe immediate infusion-related reaction in carefully selected patients once suspected pulmonary toxicity has fully resolved. Desensitization should not be interpreted as protection against recurrent drug-induced pneumonitis and requires individualized risk-benefit assessment, allergy evaluation, pulmonary reassessment, and administration in a specialized setting.

title: Beyond Pattern Recognition Artificial Intelligence for Integrated Diagnosis of Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma.
abstract: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) remains one of the most diagnostically complex malignancies because accurate diagnosis requires the integration of heterogeneous evidence from imaging, endoscopy, histopathology, molecular testing, and clinical evaluation rather than interpretation of any single modality in isolation. Artificial intelligence (AI) has shown promising performance across individual diagnostic tasks, including lesion detection, lymph node assessment, digital pathology, and biomarker prediction. Nevertheless, these advances have translated only modestly into routine clinical practice. In this Review, we examine AI in HNSCC from the perspective of diagnostic capability rather than algorithmic performance. We argue that a key challenge for current AI systems is moving beyond multimodal data integration or classification toward clinical reasoning. Here, clinical reasoning refers to the patient-level synthesis of heterogeneous diagnostic evidence in clinical context, including the interpretation of concordant and conflicting findings and associated uncertainty. We summarize recent advances in imaging, endoscopy, digital pathology, molecular analysis, multimodal learning, and foundation models, while critically evaluating their clinical strengths and limitations. We further discuss the major barriers to clinical translation, including limited generalizability, insufficient prospective and external validation, workflow integration, regulatory considerations, and clinician trust. Emerging multimodal AI and foundation models represent important steps toward patient-level evidence integration, yet current systems remain predominantly designed for isolated pattern recognition rather than diagnostic synthesis. Future progress should therefore focus on developing and prospectively validating AI systems that can integrate heterogeneous diagnostic evidence at the individual-patient level while preserving uncertainty and clinical oversight. At present, integrated clinical reasoning remains a research objective rather than an established capability of AI in HNSCC diagnosis.

title: An Update on Blood-Brain Barrier Penetrating Nanoparticles for the Treatment of Glioblastoma.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive and lethal primary brain malignancy, with patient survival largely unchanged over recent decades despite advances in surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy. A major therapeutic challenge is the blood-brain barrier (BBB), which restricts the delivery of many systemically administered drugs, including emerging biologic and gene-based therapies. Nanoparticle (NP) delivery systems have therefore attracted intense interest to overcome BBB-associated transport limitations, enhance tumor specificity and enable delivery of potent therapeutic cargos to infiltrative GBM cells. This review provides an overview of some recent advances in BBB-penetrating NP platforms for GBM treatment, spanning lipid-based, polymeric, dendrimer, inorganic, peptide-based and biomimetic systems. We discuss several extracellular and intracellular biological barriers to effective delivery, while outlining how these challenges may inform rational NP design. Targeting strategies exploiting a range of receptors are reviewed alongside stimuli-responsive systems and combination approaches that integrate BBB modulation techniques, including focused ultrasound and intranasal nose-to-brain delivery. While many NP platforms demonstrate compelling preclinical efficacy, translation to the clinic remains limited. We therefore discuss recent clinical developments and highlight select translational opportunities such as preclinical model selection, manufacturing scalability factors and regulatory considerations. As such there may be a need for integrated design strategies, clinically relevant model systems and robust biodistribution and toxicity assessment. Aligning advances in nanotechnology with GBM biology and clinical constraints may be essential in realizing the therapeutic promise of BBB-penetrating nanomedicines to improve outcomes for patients with this devastating disease. Collectively, BBB-penetrating NPs may represent a promising strategy for GBM treatment, and bridging the gap between preclinical success and clinical benefit may remain an opportunity for the field.

title: Visceral and Ectopic Fat Remodeling with Incretin-Based Therapies in Type 2 Diabetes: Human Imaging Evidence.
abstract: Incretin-based therapies change the distribution of adipose tissue and ectopic lipid during weight loss. This narrative review examines human imaging evidence across abdominal, hepatic, pancreatic, cardiac and skeletal-muscle fat during treatment with selective glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists and dual- and triple-receptor agonists. Adults with type 2 diabetes are the primary population; findings from mixed diabetes populations and obesity-related disorders are identified separately. The central question is how depot responses relate to overall weight loss and organ outcomes. Hepatic fat has the most mature evidence, and visceral-fat reduction is supported across multiple studies. Tirzepatide provides the most extensive linked multi-depot imaging dataset, while recent survodutide findings extend GLP-1/glucagon imaging evidence to abdominal fat in obesity without diabetes. Cardiac and skeletal-muscle studies extend assessment to tissue composition and ventricular remodeling; pancreatic, renal sinus and other perivascular responses remain exploratory. Imaging modality, anatomical coverage, segmentation and endpoint definition vary across studies, and receptor comparisons are uneven in their populations, comparators and depots assessed. Remodeling is predominantly weight-associated, with selected studies identifying disproportionate hepatic or visceral responses. Imaging can connect these responses to the organ phenotype of interest: hepatic disease activity, cardiac structure or muscle composition. The next step is to test whether repeated depot measurements improve prediction of functional and clinical outcomes beyond routine weight and metabolic assessment.

title: Epidural Steroid Injection Approaches Across the Spine: A Practical Narrative Review of Technique, Indications, and Contrast Patterns.
abstract: Background Epidural steroid injection (ESI) is among the most frequently performed image-guided interventions for spinal pain. The strongest evidence supports its use for radicular pain, particularly lumbar radicular pain from disc herniation, while evidence for nonspecific axial or discogenic pain is weaker and approach-dependent. The route used to reach the epidural space (caudal, interlaminar, or transforaminal) has major implications for drug distribution, effectiveness, and safety. Objective and scope This narrative review offers a practical overview of considerations for performing ESI in the cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and sacral regions, integrating the authors' clinical experience with current medical society guidance. We describe the relevant anatomy, techniques, indications, and limitations of the various approaches. Techniques and approaches Particular attention is given to the transforaminal approach, contrasting the subpedicular ("safe triangle") technique with the infraneural (Kambin/retrodiscal) technique, a distinction that applies primarily to thoracolumbar injection; to the contralateral oblique (CLO) view for interlaminar depth assessment; and to caudal delivery under fluoroscopic and ultrasound guidance. Contrast patterns A core section addresses the systematic recognition of an epidurogram versus off-target patterns (intravascular, intrathecal, subdural, and fascial/retrodural flow), illustrated with fluoroscopic images, since pattern recognition is central to safety and effectiveness. Safety The review summarizes corticosteroid selection, dosing and frequency, radiation protection, and antithrombotic management, and stratifies complications by frequency, severity, and approach. Where terms such as "mandatory" or "only acceptable" are used, they reflect the published recommendations of the International Pain and Spine Intervention Society (IPSIS), the World Institute of Pain (WIP) Benelux work group, or allied multisociety consensus. Conclusion Image guidance, contrast confirmation, judicious steroid selection, and etiology-driven patient selection remain the foundations of safe and effective ESI. The recommendations synthesized here represent evidence-informed expert consensus rather than high-level comparative evidence for every point.

Background

Epidural steroid injection (ESI) is among the most frequently performed image-guided interventions for spinal pain. The strongest evidence supports its use for radicular pain, particularly lumbar radicular pain from disc herniation, while evidence for nonspecific axial or discogenic pain is weaker and approach-dependent. The route used to reach the epidural space (caudal, interlaminar, or transforaminal) has major implications for drug distribution, effectiveness, and safety.

Objective and scope

This narrative review offers a practical overview of considerations for performing ESI in the cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and sacral regions, integrating the authors' clinical experience with current medical society guidance. We describe the relevant anatomy, techniques, indications, and limitations of the various approaches.

Techniques and approaches

Particular attention is given to the transforaminal approach, contrasting the subpedicular ("safe triangle") technique with the infraneural (Kambin/retrodiscal) technique, a distinction that applies primarily to thoracolumbar injection; to the contralateral oblique (CLO) view for interlaminar depth assessment; and to caudal delivery under fluoroscopic and ultrasound guidance.

Contrast patterns

A core section addresses the systematic recognition of an epidurogram versus off-target patterns (intravascular, intrathecal, subdural, and fascial/retrodural flow), illustrated with fluoroscopic images, since pattern recognition is central to safety and effectiveness.

Safety

The review summarizes corticosteroid selection, dosing and frequency, radiation protection, and antithrombotic management, and stratifies complications by frequency, severity, and approach. Where terms such as "mandatory" or "only acceptable" are used, they reflect the published recommendations of the International Pain and Spine Intervention Society (IPSIS), the World Institute of Pain (WIP) Benelux work group, or allied multisociety consensus.

Conclusion

Image guidance, contrast confirmation, judicious steroid selection, and etiology-driven patient selection remain the foundations of safe and effective ESI. The recommendations synthesized here represent evidence-informed expert consensus rather than high-level comparative evidence for every point.

title: A Longitudinal Comparison of Baseline Predictors of Five-Year OAG Development.
abstract: Purpose To compare sensitivities for prediction of development of open angle glaucoma (OAG) in 5 years in eyes initially assessed as clinically suspect open angle glaucoma in a prospective longitudinal study. Methods Data were collected prospectively every fourth month for five years from both eyes of 88 subjects with at least one clinically glaucoma suspect eye. Presently, observations at occasions 1, 2, 15 and 16 were analyzed. An eye was considered clinically glaucoma suspect eye if it met at least one of the criteria: suspicious ophthalmoscopic optic nerve head appearance, ocular hypertension, pigment dispersion syndrome, exfoliation syndrome, or visual field asymmetry. Measurements of mean deviation (MD) with standardized automatic perimetry (SAP) were used for classification of OAG at 5 years follow-up. The OAG conversion criterion was defined as a mean SAP MD below the critical limit for normality (-3.7 dB) across occasions 15 and 16. At specificity of 95% for measurement at baseline, 95% confidence intervals for sensitivity were estimated for intraocular pressure (IOP), cup-to-disc ratio (C/D-vertical) and neuro-retinal rim area (NRA), both measured with confocal scanning laser ophthalmoscopy (CSLO) and nerve fiber layer thickness measured with laser scanning polarimetry (GDx TSNIT-global) and optical coherence tomography (OCT cpRNFLT-global), respectively. Confidence intervals were estimated using Hilgers, Delta-Wald with logit transformation, and Bootstrap strategies. Results During the 5-year follow-up, 20 clinically suspect eyes met the OAG conversion criterion. The different strategies resulted in confidence intervals of the same order. The 95% confidence intervals estimated with Bootstrap strategy were 0.57 [0.30;0.84] for OCT cpRNFLT, 0.32 [0.08;0.61] for GDx TSNIT, 0.30 [0.08;0.59] for HRT NRA, 0.26 [0.05;0.58] for HRT vertical C/D, and 0.11 [0.02;0.27] for IOP. Conclusions For the currently used MD-based OAG conversion definition, OCT-cpRNFLT has the highest sensitivity for prediction of OAG development at the initial visit among the morphometric variables. The low sensitivity for IOP questions the value of IOP slightly above 21 mmHg for prediction of OAG at baseline.

title: ERBB2 Exon 20 Mutation-Guided Trastuzumab Deruxtecan Therapy in Metastatic Lung Adenocarcinoma with Low HER2 Expression: A Case Report.
abstract: HER2 mutations are uncommon in lung adenocarcinoma, and treatment options become limited after failure of standard systemic therapies. We report a 69-year-old woman with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma involving multiple lymph nodes, bone, and the left adrenal gland. Histopathological and immunohistochemical examinations strongly supported a diagnosis of primary pulmonary adenocarcinoma. Targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) performed at initial diagnosis in January 2024 identified an ERBB2 exon 20 in-frame insertion mutation (p.Y772_A775dup). The patient received six sequential treatment regimens, including platinum-based chemotherapy, PD-1 inhibitor therapy, antiangiogenic therapy, and palliative radiotherapy. Initial tumor regression was observed, but sustained disease control was not achieved. Following further disease progression, the previously identified ERBB2 mutation was reassessed by the multidisciplinary team in 2025. HER2 immunohistochemistry showed an IHC score of 1+. Based on the activating ERBB2 mutation, trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) was initiated in June 2025 at a fixed dose of 200 mg per administration (approximately 3.2 mg/kg), lower than the standard starting dose for HER2-mutant NSCLC. Five doses were administered between June and November 2025. Serum carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 levels decreased markedly after treatment. Serial chest computed tomography indicated radiological disease stabilization for approximately 5 months, with no clinically significant treatment-related adverse events documented. This case highlights the value of molecular profiling in identifying actionable ERBB2 mutations despite low HER2 protein expression. It also provides a real-world observation of disease stabilization with a lower-than-standard initial dose of T-DXd, although conclusions regarding reduced-dose efficacy cannot be drawn from a single case.

title: Effect of Ultrasound-Guided versus Conventional Lung Recruitment on End-of-Surgery Atelectasis in Adults Aged 45-74 Years Undergoing Prone-Position Spinal Surgery: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Objective This study aimed to compare the effects of ultrasound-guided stepwise lung recruitment maneuver (LRM) versus conventional manual LRM on the incidence of end-of-surgery atelectasis in patients undergoing prone-position spinal surgery. Methods In this randomized controlled trial, 120 patients aged 45-74 years undergoing prone-position spine surgery under general anesthesia were randomized to ultrasound-guided group (n = 60) or conventional manual group (n = 60). Both groups received a fixed PEEP of 5 cmH 2 O intraoperatively. The primary outcome was the incidence of ultrasound-defined atelectasis at the end of surgery (T3). Results The final analysis included 60 patients in the intervention group and 59 in the control group. title: Artificial Intelligence for Brain MRI Diagnosis: A Scoping Review and Evidence-Gap Map Across Neurological Diseases.
abstract: Introduction/objective Artificial Intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, is increasingly applied to brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) for disease detection, classification, segmentation, and clinically relevant prediction. This review aimed to map the evidence on AI-assisted brain MRI diagnosis, identify methodological and clinical translation gaps, and propose priorities for future research. Methods This scoping review was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science were searched for peer-reviewed English-language publications from January 2018 to April 2026. Data were charted according to disease domain, study design, AI method, dataset, validation strategy, performance metrics, explainability, and key limitations. Results The search identified 1,020 records. After duplicate removal and screening, 61 publications were included, comprising 24 original studies used for the primary evidence map and 37 reviews or commentaries used for contextual synthesis. Evidence was strongest for brain tumor imaging and Alzheimer's disease, whereas stroke, multiple sclerosis, pediatric neuroimaging, and rare neurological conditions were underrepresented. Most studies relied on public benchmark datasets and retrospective validation, whereas external validation, prospective clinical evaluation, subgroup analysis, explainability, and workflow integration were inconsistently reported. Discussion The findings indicate that AI-assisted brain MRI research remains unevenly developed and is constrained by dataset dependence, limited external validation, limited prospective clinical evaluation, and inconsistent reporting of explainability, subgroup performance, and workflow integration. Conclusion AI shows promising research-stage potential for brain MRI-based diagnosis, particularly in brain tumor analysis and Alzheimer's disease classification. Future research should prioritize multicenter validation, diverse and disease-specific datasets, explainable and equitable AI design, transparent reporting, and prospective evaluation within real clinical workflows.

title: Primary Male Appendiceal Choriocarcinoma With Background of Low-Grade Appendiceal Mucinous Neoplasm: Diagnostic Challenges and Poor Prognosis.
abstract: Background/aim Choriocarcinoma is a highly aggressive trophoblastic malignancy that is most commonly gestational in origin. Non-gestational choriocarcinoma in the male gastrointestinal tract is extremely rare, and primary appendiceal involvement is exceptional. Case report We report such a case of a 75-year-old male who presented to the emergency room with severe abdominal pain. Physical examination indicated possible acute appendicitis suspicious for perforation, and computed tomography (CT) scans revealed a 7.5 cm mass in the lower right quadrant as well as numerous liver hypoechoic nodules. No lesions/nodules were identified in his testicles or mediastinum. Emergency surgery with right hemicolectomy and concurrent liver biopsy was performed. Pathology gross exam revealed a 7.5 cm appendiceal mass with associated appendiceal perforation. Histologically, the tumor showed a poorly differentiated carcinoma morphologically composed of syncytiotrophoblasts, cytotrophoblasts and intermediate trophoblasts with adjacent low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm (LAMN). The carcinoma cells were positive for cytokeratin 7 (CK7), beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG), GATA-binding protein 3 (GATA 3) and Sal-like protein 4 (SALL4). These features supported a primary appendiceal choriocarcinoma and the liver biopsy demonstrated metastasis of choriocarcinoma with extensive tumor necrosis. Post-surgery lab tests also revealed an exceptionally high serum β-hCG titer of 289,308 mIU/ml. The patient underwent hospice care after surgery and expired one month later. Conclusion This is the first documented case of male primary choriocarcinoma with background of LAMN and poor prognosis. Recognition of the three carcinoma components in combination with the corresponding tumor immunohistochemical markers is the key for the precise diagnosis.

title: Performance of a Large Language Model for Predicting Clinical and Radiographic Outcomes in Knee Osteoarthritis: Single-Center Prospective Observational Study.
abstract: Background Large language models (LLMs) can extract information from unstructured clinical text, but it remains unclear whether their ability to assess current status translates into reliable predictions of longitudinal outcomes. Objective This study aimed to evaluate DeepSeek's ability to assess baseline clinical and radiographic status in knee osteoarthritis (KOA), its performance in predicting 6-month outcomes, and its interrun reproducibility. Methods This study used a single-center, prospective observational cohort design to conduct a blinded, retrospective evaluation of the LLM. A total of 128 patients with primary KOA were enrolled, of whom 111 (86.7%) completed the 6-month follow-up and were included in the primary analysis. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and a rheumatologist independently assessed KOA diagnoses, baseline Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) scores, and Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) grading based on the same standardized interview records and imaging reports and predicted 6-month outcomes. The LLM was run independently 3 times. The actual outcomes determined by another senior physician served as the reference, and the results were compared with the physician's predictions and the persistence model. Results The LLM showed high baseline diagnostic agreement with the physician (105/111, 94.6%) and good agreement on the WOMAC and KL, but 6-month predictions (WOMAC mean absolute error=5.92-6.58; KL exact agreement=74/111, 66.7%-76/111, 68.5%) were worse than those of the physician comparator (mean absolute error=3.86; 96/111, 86.5%) and not superior to those of the persistence model (mean absolute error=5.43). Despite high interrun intraclass correlation coefficients (0.982 and 0.965), exact agreement between runs was poor (35/111, 31.5% and 7/111, 6.3%). Conclusions The evaluated DeepSeek configuration may support structured baseline KOA assessment. However, its 6-month predictive accuracy and patient-level stability remain limited. Prognostic applications require evidence of added value over a persistence model.

title: A Competency Assessment Tool for Liver Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound Among Sonography Trainees: Development and Multicenter Validation Study.
abstract: Background Despite the increasing use of liver contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS), no standardized, organ-specific tool exists for assessing trainees' cognitive competency. Existing instruments lack multidimensional evaluation and external validation, which limit training quality and patient safety. Objective This study aims to develop and validate the CEUS Competency Assessment for the Liver (CCAL), a tool to standardize the evaluation of theoretical and cognitive skills in liver CEUS. Methods This retrospective cohort study had four stages: (1) item generation from literature and guidelines, (2) 3 Delphi rounds (12/21, 57.1% female experts; mean age 51.0, SD 7.2 y) and cognitive testing (10 trainees) for content validity (>85% agreement) and clarity, (3) internal validation involving 100 sonography trainees (n=66, 66% assistant professors; n=27, 27% associate professors; n=7, 7% professors; n=70, 70% CEUS-naive) with 1 month or more of training at 4 hospitals (2018-2020), and (4) external validation on 579 sonography trainees (n=299, 51.6% assistant professors; n=183, 31.6% associate professors; n=97, 16.8% professors; n=439, 75.8% CEUS-naive) with 1 or more months of training at 25 multicenter sites (2018-2020). Primary outcomes were reliability (Cronbach α and Guttman split-half) and validity (exploratory factor analysis and item discrimination), while secondary outcomes included item difficulty distribution, pass rates, and between-group differences. Results The final CCAL comprised 74 items across 3 domains (demographics: 8, self-evaluation: 13, and objective questions: 53). Internal consistency was excellent (Cronbach α=0.916 and Guttman split-half=0.908). Factor analysis confirmed a 3-factor structure explaining 74.6% of the cumulative variance. Item analysis showed a balanced difficulty distribution (35/53, 66.0% easy; 17/53, 32.1% moderate; 1/53, 1.9% difficult items). Scores varied significantly by CEUS training duration ( P <.001); trainees with 4 to 6 months or more than 6 months of training achieved higher self-evaluation ( F 2,576 =34.751, partial η²=0.108, 95% CI 0.069-0.147) and objective question ( F 2,576 =34.374, partial η²=0.107, 95% CI 0.068-0.146) scores than those with less than 3 months of training. Prior independent CEUS experience was also associated with higher scores on the self-evaluation ( t 577 =6.736, Cohen d =0.561, 95% CI 0.393-0.728; P <.001) and objective question sections ( t 577 =3.494, Cohen d =0.291, 95% CI 0.127-0.454; P =.001). Competency gaps were identified across specific competency domains: the pass rate ranged from 32.5% (188/579; image-guided intervention) to 81.3% (471/579; indications and contraindications). Conclusions The CCAL is the first liver-specific CEUS competency tool integrating objective knowledge testing with structured self-evaluation. Unlike generic or simulation-based tests, it is organ-specific and validated across a large multicenter cohort, providing a multidimensional framework that identifies specific competency gaps, most notably in advanced image-guided procedures, beyond global pass/fail outcomes. The tool supports competency-based medical education through rigorous data-driven assessment, targeted curricular improvements, cross-institutional benchmarking, and informed training standards. It evaluates cognitive competence exclusively and should not replace procedural assessment in high-stakes decisions. International validation and the establishment of criterion-related and predictive validity are essential next steps.

title: Topical Esomeprazole for the Prevention and Treatment of Radiation Dermatitis in Patients With Head and Neck Cancer: Protocol for a Phase 2 Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Background Radiation dermatitis (RD) is a common and clinically significant toxicity affecting the majority of patients undergoing external beam radiation therapy, particularly those treated for head and neck cancer (HNC). RD can impair quality of life, limit treatment intensity, and compromise oncologic outcomes; yet, there is no established standard-of-care for its prevention or management. Preclinical studies suggest that a topically reformulated proton pump inhibitor (PPI), esomeprazole (Dermaprazole), has antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antifibrotic properties that may mitigate radiation-induced skin injury. Objective This phase 2 randomized controlled trial aims to evaluate the potential safety, feasibility, and efficacy of prophylactic topical Dermaprazole compared with standard supportive care (Aquaphor) in reducing the incidence and severity of clinically significant RD in patients with HNC receiving definitive chemoradiation. Methods This is a prospective, single-center, randomized controlled trial with a 2:1 allocation ratio. A total of 45 adults (≥18 y) with biopsy-confirmed head and neck malignancy planned to receive definitive chemoradiation of at least 66 Gy will be enrolled. Participants will be randomized to receive twice-daily topical Dermaprazole or Aquaphor beginning at computed tomography (CT) simulation and continuing through 2 weeks after completion of radiation therapy. The primary outcome is the rate and severity of RD, assessed weekly during treatment using the National Cancer Institute (NCI) Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 5 by the treating radiation oncologist, with blinded dermatologic assessment based on standardized medical photography. Feasibility outcomes include accrual rate, treatment compliance, and questionnaire completion rates. Secondary outcomes include time to onset and healing of grade ≥2 RD, quality of life assessed using the Skindex-16 instrument, radiation dose thresholds associated with dermatitis, and changes in inflammatory biomarkers (C-reactive protein, tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin [IL]-1β, and IL-6). More specifically, secondary outcomes will be assessed through serial CTCAE version 5 evaluations for onset and healing, Skindex16 questionnaires for quality of life, radiation dose-volume parameters for dermatitis thresholds, and serum inflammatory marker concentration measurements before, during, and after treatment. Results The study began in June 2022 and has completed enrollment. Data analysis will commence following completion of data collection, with results expected to be published by 2027. Conclusions Should Dermaprazole demonstrate efficacy in reducing RD in patients undergoing radiation therapy, it may offer an alternative or adjunctive treatment option for the prevention and management of RD, potentially reducing treatment-related morbidity and improving patients' quality of life during radiotherapy. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04865731; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04865731. International registered report identifier (irrid) DERR1-10.2196/91035.

This phase 2 randomized controlled trial aims to evaluate the potential safety, feasibility, and efficacy of prophylactic topical Dermaprazole compared with standard supportive care (Aquaphor) in reducing the incidence and severity of clinically significant RD in patients with HNC receiving definitive chemoradiation.

Methods

This is a prospective, single-center, randomized controlled trial with a 2:1 allocation ratio. A total of 45 adults (≥18 y) with biopsy-confirmed head and neck malignancy planned to receive definitive chemoradiation of at least 66 Gy will be enrolled. Participants will be randomized to receive twice-daily topical Dermaprazole or Aquaphor beginning at computed tomography (CT) simulation and continuing through 2 weeks after completion of radiation therapy. The primary outcome is the rate and severity of RD, assessed weekly during treatment using the National Cancer Institute (NCI) Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 5 by the treating radiation oncologist, with blinded dermatologic assessment based on standardized medical photography. Feasibility outcomes include accrual rate, treatment compliance, and questionnaire completion rates. Secondary outcomes include time to onset and healing of grade ≥2 RD, quality of life assessed using the Skindex-16 instrument, radiation dose thresholds associated with dermatitis, and changes in inflammatory biomarkers (C-reactive protein, tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin [IL]-1β, and IL-6). More specifically, secondary outcomes will be assessed through serial CTCAE version 5 evaluations for onset and healing, Skindex16 questionnaires for quality of life, radiation dose-volume parameters for dermatitis thresholds, and serum inflammatory marker concentration measurements before, during, and after treatment.

Results

The study began in June 2022 and has completed enrollment. Data analysis will commence following completion of data collection, with results expected to be published by 2027.

Conclusions

Should Dermaprazole demonstrate efficacy in reducing RD in patients undergoing radiation therapy, it may offer an alternative or adjunctive treatment option for the prevention and management of RD, potentially reducing treatment-related morbidity and improving patients' quality of life during radiotherapy.

title: The Digital Twin Paradigm in Head and Neck Cancer: Clinical Opportunities and Challenges.
abstract: Unlabelled Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) represents a significant public health challenge. Its treatment is characterized by high anatomical complexity and a critical need for functional preservation of speech, swallowing, and respiration. While multimodality care, including surgery, radiotherapy, and systemic therapy, has substantially improved patient survival, there are still high rates of life-altering toxicities and low response rates to immunotherapy. Current clinical decision-making largely relies on "digital snapshots"-static representations derived from population-based statistics and time point-specific imaging-which usually fail to account for the rapid anatomical and biological change during the course of treatment. Digital twins hold great promise in accelerating scientific breakthroughs and transforming oncology treatment and precision medicine through the creation of high-fidelity virtual patient representations that integrate real-time biological, anatomical, and clinical data. In this viewpoint, we propose 3 interconnected digital twins to establish a conceptual framework for the HNSCC digital twin. These digital twins include the anatomical twin, using virtual surgical planning and augmented reality for geometric precision; the dosimetric twin, using daily imaging and synthetic computed tomography generation for automated adaptive radiotherapy; and the biological twin, integrating deep phenotyping, radiomics, and mechanistic omics to simulate individualized therapeutic trajectories. Beyond acute care, we explore the clinical utility of digital twins in navigating the "de-escalation dilemma" for human papillomavirus-associated disease and improving survivorship through digital phenotyping. With the advent of longitudinal data from medical-grade Internet-of-Things sensors and circulating tumor DNA kinetics, digital twins can serve as active sentinels, detecting functional decline or subclinical events months before clinical manifestation. Furthermore, the implementation of synthetic control arms via virtual populations offers an avenue to accelerate clinical trials and address ethical issues in rare molecular subtypes. Despite this potential, substantial barriers to implementation remain, including profound anatomical instability during treatment, the "black box" nature of deep learning algorithms, and the challenges of multiscale data integration. We provide a technical roadmap for the development of "morphing" digital twins-dynamic systems capable of continuous geometric and biological auditing. By bridging the gap between the macroscopic world of radiation physics and the microscopic world of cellular evolution, digital twins may help shift the management of HNSCC from population-based statistical probability toward more individualized, biologically informed decision-making, with the goal of optimizing HNSCC management while preserving essential patient functions.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Fine-Grained Image-Interpretation Performance of Multimodal Large Language Models on Bilingual Radiology Questions: Cross-Sectional Benchmark Study.
abstract: Background Multimodal large language models (LLMs) are rapidly expanding in radiology and digital health; however, their diagnostic performance across diverse clinical scenarios and fine-grained visual reasoning tasks requires systematic evaluation. Objective The study aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and fine-grained visual reasoning performance of 5 multimodal LLMs with bilingual medical imaging questions. Methods This cross-sectional benchmark study evaluated bilingual medical imaging questions using zero-shot prompting on 5 LLMs: GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro, Doubao, Yuanbao, and Llama 4 Maverick. Subgroup analyses by language (English/Chinese), question type (image/text), imaging modality (computed tomography, radiography, magnetic resonance imaging, ultrasound, and nuclear medicine), and anatomical system (neurologic, respiratory, cardiovascular, digestive, genitourinary, and musculoskeletal) evaluated intermodel accuracy and intramodel consistency. Image-based visual reasoning performance was assessed across modality, anatomy, lesion detection, and localization. Results A total of 298 questions (198 image-based, 100 text-based) were evaluated. Gemini 3 Pro achieved the highest overall accuracy (n=268, 89.9%, 95% CI 86.0%-92.9%), significantly outperforming Doubao (n=235, 78.9%; P <.001), GPT-5.2 (n=233, 78.2%; P <.001), Yuanbao (n=216, 72.5%; P <.001), and Llama 4 Maverick (n=216, 72.5%; P <.001). All models performed better on text-based than image-based questions (Yuanbao, P <.001; Doubao, P =.02; GPT-5.2, P <.001; Gemini 3 Pro, P =.002; Llama 4 Maverick, P <.001). GPT-5.2 ( P <.001), Llama 4 Maverick ( P =.03), and Yuanbao ( P =.03) favored English questions, while intramodel performance remained stable across modalities (Yuanbao, P =.46; Doubao, P =.21; GPT-5.2, P =.26; Gemini 3 Pro, P =.96; Llama 4 Maverick, P =.45) and anatomical systems (Yuanbao, P =.82; Doubao, P =.52; GPT-5.2, P =.35; Gemini 3 Pro, P =.13; Llama 4 Maverick, P =.97). Despite near-perfect macroscopic visual recognition (modality and anatomy: 99.0%-100.0%), accuracy dropped in complex tasks. Gemini 3 Pro outperformed Yuanbao ( P <.001), GPT-5.2 ( P =.002), and Llama 4 Maverick ( P <.001) in lesion detection (175/198, 88.4%) and outperformed Yuanbao ( P <.001), Doubao ( P =.004), and Llama 4 Maverick ( P =.004) in lesion localization (189/198, 95.5%). Conclusions Gemini 3 Pro demonstrated optimal, comprehensive performance and cross-lingual stability. However, current multimodal LLMs face a technical bottleneck in complex visual interpretation-particularly in fine-grained lesion detection and localization-emphasizing the need to prioritize local feature perception in future model development.

title: Expert Perspectives on Transparency and Trust in AI-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems for Chest X-Ray Diagnosis: Qualitative Study.
abstract: Background The integration of AI-based Clinical Decision Support Systems (AI-CDSS) into clinical practice has expanded rapidly, particularly in medical imaging. Beyond algorithmic performance, growing evidence suggests that clinicians' engagement with AI-CDSS is shaped by how transparently systems communicate their outputs, and how trust is formed through human-AI interaction. However, a limited understanding of how these concepts are perceived by end users and developers continues to hinder real-world implementation. Objective This study aims to explore expert perspectives on transparency and trust in AI-CDSS for chest X-ray diagnosis, with a focus on the two-dimensional lens: user interface and users' mental models. Methods A qualitative study was conducted using semistructured interviews with a total of 21 experts, including 11 radiologists and 10 AI experts experienced in AI-CDSS. Data were analyzed thematically to explore factors perceived to influence transparent communication and trust. Results Three themes emerged: (1) perspective of transparency and trust, (2) user interface, and (3) users' mental models. Findings reveal that trust is a dynamic calibration process developed through repeated use, feedback loops, and alignment with clinicians' mental models, rather than algorithmic accuracy alone. Significant discrepancies were identified between how developers design system transparency and how clinicians interpret AI outputs. Conclusions This study demonstrates that transparency and trust are achieved through interpretable outputs, clear communication of system limitations, and alignment with clinical workflows. Designing trustworthy AI-CDSS requires integrating transparent interface design with consideration of users' knowledge, experience, and attitudes to support effective human-AI interaction.

title: Patient-Specific Virtual Reality for Lumbar Decompression Surgery: An Automated Imaging Pipeline and Educational Assessment
abstract: Manual construction of patient-specific models has limited the use of virtual reality (VR) for case-specific spine surgical rehearsal, and simulator assessments are often not patient-specific. We present a largely automated pipeline that converts routine preoperative CT and MRI into patient-specific 3D models for VR rehearsal of lumbar decompression, paired with case-specific written assessments. CT was segmented with an unmodified vertebral network and MRI with an in-house nnU-Net; volumes were registered and exported for VR. A locally hosted large language model generated per-case assessments from each patient's radiology report; the pipeline ran in approximately two minutes per case, and MRI segmentation reached a mean Dice of 0.870. Eight patient-specific models were prepared, and eleven trainees (undergraduate to fellow) completed a faculty-guided session with pre/post knowledge testing. Knowledge scores increased from 5.82 to 7.27 out of 10 (Wilcoxon $p=0.008$; Cohen's $d=1.01$), with 8 of 11 improving and none declining, and trainees rated educational value favorably. This feasibility study demonstrates a fast, fully private pipeline producing patient-specific VR models and matched assessments; the educational findings are preliminary and uncontrolled, motivating a larger controlled trial.

title: Feasibility of Augmented Reality-Guided Robotic Ultrasound with Cone-Beam CT Integration for Spine Procedures
abstract: Needle placement in spine interventions is critical for effective pain management, yet it depends on reliable identification of anatomical landmarks and careful trajectory planning. Conventional imaging guidance often relies on both computed tomography (CT) and X-ray fluoroscopy, exposing patients and staff to high doses of radiation while providing limited real-time 3D feedback. The choice of visualization may also affect operator performance and cognitive workload. We present an optical see-through augmented reality (OST-AR)–guided robotic system for spine procedures that provides in situ visualization of spinal structures to support needle trajectory planning. We integrate a cone-beam CT (CBCT)-derived 3D spine model, which is co-registered with live ultrasound, enabling users to combine global anatomical context with local, real-time imaging. We evaluated the system in a phantom user study involving two representative spine procedures: facet joint injection and lumbar puncture. Sixteen participants performed insertions under two visualization conditions: conventional screen vs. AR. Results show that AR significantly reduces execution time and across-task placement error, while also improving usability, trust, and spatial understanding, and lowering cognitive workload. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of AR-guided robotic ultrasound for spine interventions, highlighting its potential to enhance accuracy, efficiency, and user experience in image-guided procedures.

title: Prevalence and morphological types of middle mesial canals in mandibular molars according to the Barros-Costa classification: a CBCT study in a Turkish subpopulation.
abstract: Objective The purpose of this study was to assess the prevalence and configurations of middle mesial canals (MMCs) in a Turkish subpopulation using cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) according to the Barros-Costa classification. Materials and methods Two experienced endodontists assessed the prevalence of MMCs in mandibular molars of 213 Turkish patients aged 18-65 years (111 females, 102 males). MMCs were categorized using the Barros-Costa classification based on their association with the mesiobuccal and mesiolingual canals using CBCT scans in all three planes. Chi-square and Fisher's exact tests were used for unadjusted comparisons (p < 0.05). A multivariable generalized estimating equations (GEE) model with patient ID as the clustering variable was used to assess the associations between MMC presence and tooth type, age, and sex. Results Of 589 mandibular molars evaluated, 12.4% had an MMC. Distribution was: mesiolingual confluent (43.8%), mesiobuccal confluent (24.7%), independent (23.3%), and confluent (8.2%). MMCs were significantly more frequent in mandibular first molars (20.6%) than in second molars (6.6%) (p < 0.001). The most frequently observed MMC type was the mesiolingual confluent. In the multivariable GEE analysis, mandibular first molars had significantly higher odds of presenting an MMC than second molars (adjusted odds ratio = 3.54, 95% confidence interval: 2.16-5.80, p < 0.001), whereas age and sex were not significantly associated with MMC presence. Conclusions Within the examined single-center Turkish subpopulation and under the specific CBCT acquisition protocol used, MMCs were detected more frequently in mandibular first molars than in second molars. The mesiolingual confluent configuration was the most frequently observed morphological type. These findings highlight the anatomical variability of MMCs and support careful assessment of the mesial root canal system during endodontic treatment.
