title: Axillary Malignant Peripheral Nerve Sheath Tumor With Aggressive Clinical Course: A Case Report.
abstract: Aim Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST) involvement of the axillary region is exceptionally uncommon and poses significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Case presentation We report the case of a 41-year-old woman who presented with a left axillary mass initially detected during pregnancy. Imaging revealed a large axillary lesion closely associated with neurovascular structures. Histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses supported an MPNST diagnosis. Despite multimodal management, including partial surgical resection, combination chemotherapy with ifosfamide/doxorubicin-based regimens, radiotherapy, repeated surgical interventions, and reconstructive procedures, the disease demonstrated aggressive behavior with multiple local recurrences, nodal and cutaneous metastases, and an eventual mass in the gluteal region. Results MPNSTs account for 3-10% of soft tissue sarcomas and are frequently associated with poor outcomes, particularly in tumors larger than 5 cm, high-grade lesions, and those associated with neurofibromatosis type 1. Diagnosis relies on a combination of histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and advanced imaging modalities. Complete surgical resection with negative margins remains the only potentially curative treatment; however, this is often not feasible due to tumor location and extent. Radiotherapy may improve local control, while chemotherapy has limited efficacy in advanced disease. Conclusions Axillary MPNST is an exceedingly rare entity with an aggressive clinical course and poor prognosis. This case highlights the challenges in management and underscores the need for early diagnosis, aggressive multimodal treatment, and the development of more effective systemic and targeted therapies.

title: Efficacy and Prognostic Analysis of Neuro-Navigation Robot-Assisted Puncture Drainage for Thalamic Hemorrhage: A Comparison With Neuro-Endoscopy and External Ventricular Drainage.
abstract: Aim This study aims to compare the clinical efficacy of three surgical techniques-robot-assisted neuro-navigation, external ventricular drainage (EVD), and neuro-endoscopy-in evacuating intracranial hematomas in patients with thalamic hemorrhage. Methods This retrospective study included 110 patients, divided into three groups based on the surgical method: robot group ( n = 30), EVD group ( n = 37), and neuro-endoscopy group ( n = 43). Baseline characteristics, perioperative parameters, neurological function, inflammatory response, complications, and functional outcomes were compared and analyzed among the three patient groups. Results Compared with the EVD and neuro-endoscopy groups, the robot group had shorter operative times ( p < 0.001), higher hematoma clearance rates ( p < 0.001), better postoperative neurological function ( p < 0.05), a lower inflammatory response ( p < 0.05), fewer complications ( p < 0.05), and better functional outcomes ( p < 0.05). Robot-assisted neuro-navigation-guided puncture drainage was associated with better clinical outcomes than EVD and neuro-endoscopy in this retrospective study. Conclusions Robot-assisted neuro-navigation-guided puncture drainage was associated with improved neurological recovery and short-term outcomes in patients with thalamic hemorrhage.

title: Risk Factors for Bone Cement Leakage and Re-fracture Following PKP in Patients With Thoracolumbar Spine Fractures.
abstract: Aim Thoracolumbar spine fractures are commonly treated with percutaneous kyphoplasty (PKP), but bone cement leakage and re-fracture remain major concerns. Identifying their risk factors is essential for improving prognosis but remains insufficiently characterized. This study was designed to explore the risk factors for bone cement leakage and re-fracture following PKP in patients with thoracolumbar spine fractures. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 115 patients with thoracolumbar spine fractures who underwent PKP at Heilongjiang Provincial Hospital between April 2022 and February 2025 (leakage group: 18 patients with bone cement leakage; non-leakage group: 97 patients without leakage). Risk factors for bone cement leakage were analyzed. Patients were divided into re-fracture (29 cases with re-fractures) and non-re-fracture (86 cases without re-fractures) groups to identify risk factors for postoperative re-fracture. Results Logistic multivariate regression analysis identified age and vertebral wall destruction as independent risk factors for postoperative bone cement leakage ( p < 0.05). Separately, age, the degree of vertebral compression, and vertebral wall destruction were identified as independent risk factors for re-fracture after surgery ( p < 0.05). Conclusions Age and vertebral wall destruction are independent predictors of cement leakage, and together with compression severity, also predict re-fracture. These findings support routine preoperative assessment of vertebral wall integrity using high-resolution computed tomography (CT), particularly in elderly patients, as vertebral wall destruction was independently associated with bone cement leakage.

title: Dense Breast Tissue Segmentation under Limited Annotation: Comparing CNNs, Transformers, Self-Supervision, and Prompting
abstract: Dense breast tissue reduces the sensitivity of mammographic screening and is an important risk factor for breast cancer, making accurate dense-tissue segmentation particularly important when expert pixel-level annotations are limited. We empirically study dense breast tissue segmentation under limited pixel-level supervision using a small expert-annotated dataset (596 images) together with an in-domain unlabeled mammography dataset (20,000 images). We compare classical pixel-level segmentation methods, CNN and U-Net encoder-decoder models, transformer-based models, self-supervised pre-training, fine-tuning strategies, loss functions, and prompt-based MedSAM variants under a unified evaluation protocol. CNN-based models achieve the best standalone segmentation performance while providing the most favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost. In contrast, the adaptive fuzzy c-means + SVM baseline and transformer-based models perform worse in this low-label setting. Our analysis of prompt-based MedSAM further shows that SAM-style models are highly sensitive to prompt quality. Box and breast-region prompts lead to poor performance, whereas CNN-generated dense prompts substantially improve MedSAM performance. However, even with mask-decoder fine-tuning, CNN-prompted MedSAM does not outperform the best standalone CNN model, suggesting that current SAM-style models require stronger prompts or adaptation beyond the mask decoder for diffuse breast-density segmentation. Additionally, a density-calibrated hybrid loss primarily improves percentdensity calibration by reducing the test MAE from 14.8 to 11.8 percentage points. Our computational cost analysis indicates that many generic self-supervised learning and parameter-efficient adaptation strategies provide limited practical benefit relative to their additional cost. These findings offer practical guidance for developing reproducible dense breast tissue segmentation models in mammography studies with limited labeled data.

title: Cross-Scanner Reliability of Brain MRI Foundation Models: A Travelling-Heads Study
abstract: Foundation models (FMs) are increasingly used for brain MRI analysis, but their reliability across scanners remains unclear. We evaluated seven FMs using 120 acquisitions from 20 participants in the ON-Harmony travelling-heads dataset. We also used a separate cohort of 1,411 healthy adults to train brain-age predictors, either by fitting Ridge regression to frozen embeddings or by fine-tuning the models. We assessed how accurately they predicted age and how consistently their embeddings and age predictions behaved across scanners. AnatCL and y-Aware produced the most reliable embeddings, with distance-based intraclass correlation coefficients (dbICC) of 0.91-0.92, approaching 0.95 for FreeSurfer-derived anatomical measurements. Their shared anatomical preprocessing emerged as a plausible contributor to this pattern. Ridge predictions had higher dbICC than full embeddings for NeuroVFM (0.88 versus 0.19) and Curia-2 (0.84 versus 0.16). After fine-tuning, predictions for the same person differed between scanners by approximately 2 years on average for AnatCL and y-Aware, compared with 4-6 years for NeuroVFM and Curia-2. After correction for multiple comparisons, fine-tuning improved internal-test accuracy in three of seven models and reduced absolute cross-scanner differences in two. These findings favour anatomically focused models for reliable predictions, while highlighting the challenge of preserving useful image information without sacrificing cross-scanner reliability.

title: ConfUSIus: an accessible and scalable toolkit for functional ultrasound imaging analysis
abstract: Functional ultrasound imaging (fUSI) maps brainwide hemodynamics at high resolution, yet analysis requires expert knowledge as pipelines remain fragmented across laboratories. We introduce ConfUSIus, an open-source Python package and graphical interface for accessible, scalable, and reproducible fUSI analysis. Its common data model unifies heterogeneous fUSI recordings across beamformed IQ processing, motion correction, registration, denoising, and statistical analysis. ConfUSIus lowers barriers and facilitates method development, comparison, and sharing.

title: Cerebrovascular Structure–Flow Gradients Revealed by Volumetric Ultrasound Localization Microscopy
abstract: Characterizing the joint organization of microscale cerebrovascular structure and flow in vivo is challenging. Volumetric ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) provides spatially resolved measures of microvascular structure and flow from the same acquisition, but how these features are jointly organized across brain networks remains unclear. Here, we characterized local vascular phenotypes from transcranial volumetric ULM in mice and examined whether they contained reproducible low-dimensional organization. Local measures of vascular structure and flow dynamics were summarized within corresponding brain regions across mice. Subject-specific vascular phenotype similarity matrices were combined into a group-consensus graph and analyzed using diffusion embedding. Two leading gradients, showing distinct spatial distributions across brain networks, were reproducibly recovered across subject and spatial scales. The principal gradient was associated with local vascular density and flow complexity, defining a vascular structure-related axis. The secondary gradient was associated with flow speed and acceleration, defining a flow-dynamics-related axis. These gradients provide a low-dimensional representation of the cerebrovascular structure and flow and provide a reference for studying coordinated vascular changes across disease, aging, and intervention.

title: Real-time Volumetric Imaging for Minimally-Invasive Thoracic Interventions: A Deformable Phantom Study
abstract: ObjectivesThis study aimed to evaluate the ability of VoxelMap, a deep learning framework for 3D respiratory motion estimation, to generate volumetric images in real-time from 2D projections acquired for two deformable lung phantoms on a clinical interventional C-arm angiography system. Materials and MethodsVoxelMap was evaluated using the PixelPrint4D and Casper deformable physical thoracic respiratory phantoms. Four-dimensional cone-beam CT (4D CBCT) images acquired on a clinical fixed-room C-arm angiography system were used for network training and volumetric ground truth. Prediction accuracy was evaluated on withheld respiratory phases using structural similarity index measure (SSIM) and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR). Model inference time was measured to assess suitability for continuous real-time processing. Deep ensembles were also used to assess model uncertainty. Correlation between ensemble uncertainty and prediction error was evaluated for both phantoms. ResultsVoxelMap achieved high prediction accuracy across withheld respiratory phases in both physical phantoms. SSIM values exceeded 0.92 in all experiments, with a higher performance observed for the Casper phantom (0.969-0.973) than for the PixelPrint4D phantom (0.927-0.943). Model inference times were less than 15 ms for both phantoms which is compatible with real-time processing. Ensemble uncertainty was positively correlated with prediction error in both phantoms, indicating that higher uncertainty was associated with less accurate volumetric predictions. ConclusionsOur study demonstrated that VoxelMap generates accurate volumetric deformations of respiratory anatomy from projections acquired on a clinical interventional C-arm system, with computational inference times compatible with continuous processing. By deriving volumetric information directly from two-dimensional fluoroscopic projections, VoxelMap has the potential to augment continuous fluoroscopic guidance with continuously updated volumetric information. Ensemble uncertainty may provide a potentially useful indicator of prediction reliability. Further studies using clinically representative training data and patient studies is required to establish clinical utility. Our code is available at https://github.com/Image-X-Institute/Voxelmap.

title: Topographic reference modelling of white matter hyperintensities across the adult lifespan
abstract: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are among the most common MRI findings in older adults. They are widely regarded as markers of brain aging and cerebral small-vessel disease, and associated with risk for cognitive decline, Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD), and stroke. White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are typically interpreted by total lesion burden, but lesions with similar volumes can occupy different anatomical locations, potentially reflecting distinct pathological processes. Here we present voxelwise topographic reference modelling (vTRM), a framework for characterizing individual WMH masks against age- and sex-stratified frequency maps derived from cognitively unimpaired individuals. Using 42,469 FLAIR-derived lesion masks from twelve adult cohorts, we mapped population-level WMH spatial vulnerability, characterized age-related changes in its distribution across periventricular, lobar and arterial-territory compartments, and constructed paired percentile charts for lesion burden and spatial typicality. A quadrant-based classification defined by these two percentile dimensions revealed graded relationships with ADRD pathophysiology, neurodegeneration, and cognitive impairment, while identifying WMH patterns differentially associated with ageing-related, vascular and neurodegenerative processes among individuals with similar lesion volumes. These reference charts establish a benchmark for normative WMH ageing, enabling quantification of individual deviations from typical age-, sex- and burden-related patterns and identification of WMH phenotypes associated with vascular, neurodegenerative or mixed etiologies. The framework, together with a deployable 3D U-Net model trained on these data for automated WMH segmentation, is available through the Brain Lesion Analytics platform ( https://brainlesionanalytics.org/ ).

title: Ultradeep optical coherence tomography
abstract: Deep optical imaging of intact brain tissue is limited by scattering and absorption, restricting our ability to study subcortical structures. Here, we introduce ultradeep optical coherence tomography (OCT), which combines hardware and computational approaches to enhance the signal from deep tissue regions. Ultradeep OCT utilizes a longer illumination center wavelength of 1575 nm, spectral-domain balanced detection and imaging in the conjugate configuration with the zero optical path difference positioned deep in the tissue. Autocorrelation artifacts are measured and subtracted, and multiple frames are coherently averaged to improve the signal-to-noise ratio further. These techniques, along with computational refocusing and bandwidth control, allowed us to extend structural imaging depth in biological tissues. Ultradeep OCT demonstrated physical imaging depths of 2.3 to 2.8 mm (mean 2.5 mm) in the ex vivo mouse brain and 2.5 to 3.0 mm (mean 2.8 mm) in chicken tissue. The resulting volumes in the ex vivo mouse brain samples depict the dorsal hippocampus and its two major subregions with sufficient contrast to allow segmentation and three-dimensional reconstructions. Features in the thalamus could also be discerned. These findings demonstrate the potential of ultradeep OCT as a label-free approach for visualizing deep-brain structures at a spatial scale complementary to magnetic resonance imaging and microscopy. This approach could enable optical imaging studies of hippocampal structural changes in mouse models of neurodegenerative disease.

title: Assessment of Dissemination in Time in Multiple Sclerosis Using a Single 3D T2-FLAIR magnetic resonance imaging Radiomic Signature
abstract: Background In multiple sclerosis (MS), dissemination in time (DIT) is an important component of demonstrating disease activity and establishing the chronology of lesion development. DIT is routinely assessed from contrast-enhanced or follow-up magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Although proved useful, these methods are not without caveats motivating alternative approaches to study lesion chronology. We investigated whether single T2-FLAIR MRI contains sufficient information to distinguish temporally distinct MS lesion categories using radiomic features. Methods In a retrospective longitudinal cohort of 273 participants, 39.0 (10.8) y; 172/273 female (63.0%); 101/273 male (37.0%) with MS (1,311 MRI acquisitions), persistent brain lesions were temporally stratified using serial T2-FLAIR MRI. Long-standing established (LS-E) lesions were defined as observed for six years at least, and recent incident (R-I), as lesions that appeared over the span of two years in a follow-up MRI and were present until the last scan available. Radiomic features were extracted from lesion-level T2-FLAIR MRI. Feature selection was performed in an independent discovery cohort (Group 1, N=55). Selected features were then used to train a support vector machine classifier in a separate development cohort with repeated group-wise cross-validation (Group 2, N=163). Final performance was assessed in an independent test cohort (Group 3, N=55). An exploratory analysis was then performed on baseline MRI from 64 subjects with clinically isolated syndrome (CIS), acquired after their first clinical demyelinating event. Results Group 1 comprised 55 participants with 984 classifiable lesions; paired feature selection was restricted to 32 participants who contributed both lesion categories (658 LS-E and 156 R-I lesions), yielding 18 selected radiomic features. Group 2 comprised 163 participants with 3,203 lesions. In the held-out test cohort, 55 participants contributed 814 lesions (622 LS-E and 192 R-I); the classifier achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.78 (95% CI, 0.74-0.81). Using the fixed decision threshold, 65% of R-I lesions (125/192; 95% CI, 57%-73%) and 73% of LS-E lesions (457/622; 95% CI, 69%-78%) were correctly classified. Conclusions Single T2-FLAIR MRI contains measurable information related to MS lesion chronology. This proof-of-concept framework supports the feasibility of a line of research based on radiomics temporal lesion characterisation without contrast administration or dense longitudinal follow-up MRI, with potential relevance for studying lesion evolution and supporting DIT assessment.

title: NeuroWeave-3D: Uncertainty-Aware Evidence Completion for Brain Tumor Segmentation with Missing MRI Modalities
abstract: Multi-parametric MRI segmentation models are accurate when all prescribed sequences are available but can be brittle under missing or corrupted modalities. We propose NeuroWeave-3D, a 3D glioma segmentation framework that treats missing modalities as uncertain evidence rather than deterministic channels to reconstruct. The model combines spatial modality routing, probabilistic latent feature completion, complete-to-missing consistency, and voxel-level uncertainty estimation. A curriculum over all non-empty MRI modality subsets trains one network for arbitrary sequence availability. We define a BraTS-centered evaluation that reports complete-input accuracy, macro and worst-case missing-modality performance, corruption robustness, calibration, and failure detection.

title: In-vivo MRI of noradrenergic and dopaminergic nuclei predicts future cognition and Alzheimers disease progression
abstract: Noradrenergic and dopaminergic nuclei modulate cognition, and post-mortem data indicate they are affected early in the neurodegenerative cascade of Alzheimers disease. We derived in-vivo locus coeruleus (LC) and substantia nigra-ventral tegmental area (SN-VTA) MRI integrity measures from 739 ADNI participants, examined MRI-histology correspondence in individuals with both in-vivo imaging and post-mortem data, and tested whether these measures reflect early MRI-indexed degeneration predicting later cognitive decline. LC and SN-VTA contrast predicted cognitive and behavioral function 10 years later, despite only weak associations with current function. LC- and SN-VTA-associated brain-wide atrophy patterns aligned with PET-derived norepinephrine-transporter and dopamine-receptor maps, respectively. A one-standard-deviation decrease in baseline LC contrast was associated with 84% higher five-year odds of MCI-to-AD progression, and predictive effects of the catecholaminergic nuclei were mediated by their corresponding atrophy patterns. The SN-VTA pattern was associated with less amyloid PET-related memory decline. Together, these findings establish LC and SN-VTA MRI contrast as markers of early neurodegeneration that forecast cognitive decline years before clinical onset.

title: Agreement of abdominal palpation with point-of-care ultrasound for hepatosplenic organomegaly: a cross-sectional, population-based study in schistosomiasis-endemic settings of rural Uganda
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Ultrasound is commonly used to assess hepatosplenic morbidity in schistosomiasis, but access may be limited in resource-constrained settings. Abdominal palpation is simple and inexpensive, yet its clinical value and diagnostic performance for detecting ultrasound-defined organ enlargement remains uncertain. We evaluated standardised abdominal palpation against point-of-care ultrasound in a schistosomiasis-endemic setting in rural Uganda. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional study in January-February 2024 of 3177 participants aged 5-92 years from Pakwach, Buliisa and Mayuge districts in the SchistoTrack cohort. Trained nurses who also had midwifery skills performed standardised liver and spleen palpation, assessing palpability, extension, consistency and tenderness. Palpation agreement was assessed against point-of-care B-mode ultrasound performed by sonographers with organ dimensions classified using height-standardised internal reference values. We estimated sensitivity, specificity, predictive values and Cohen’s κ for palpation against ultrasound-defined liver and spleen enlargement and assessed associations between liver consistency and tenderness, and schistosomal periportal fibrosis examined from ultrasound. Results Spleen palpation had high specificity (98.4%), with sensitivity ranging from 10.9% for moderate splenomegaly to 48.6% for severe splenomegaly. There was strong agreement with ultrasound for severe splenomegaly (κ=0.57) though weak agreement for moderate splenomegaly (κ=0.14). Liver palpation had high specificity (97.7%) but very low sensitivity (3.4-7.3%) and minimal agreement with any hepatomegaly found from ultrasound (κ=0.02-0.04). Among participants with a palpable liver, schistosomal periportal fibrosis was more frequent in those with firm/hard than soft liver consistency (53.3%, n=24/45 vs 8.6%, n=3/35; χ²=17.64, p<0.001); while tenderness was not associated with schistosomal periportal fibrosis. Nurses additionally identified clinically relevant findings, including umbilical collaterals, abdominal swelling, and abdominal or hypochondrial pain and tenderness. Conclusions Standardised abdominal palpation cannot replace ultrasound for comprehensive detection or exclusion of hepatosplenomegaly. Nevertheless, severe ultrasound-defined splenomegaly was more readily detected by palpation, while liver consistency and other clinical findings provided information beyond organomegaly. In schistosomiasis-endemic settings with limited access to ultrasound, further research is needed to assess building capacity for abdominal palpation and how it can be combined with clinical information to increase clinical suspicion while possibly informing low-cost strategies for triage and referral.

title: Ophthalmic AI With Just Ten Examples: Comparing Multimodal Large Language Models, Vision Foundation Models, and Vision-Language Models
abstract: ABSTRACT Purpose To compare multimodal large language models (MLLMs), vision foundation models (VFMs), and contrastive vision-language models (VLMs) for ophthalmic image interpretation with no labeled examples (zero-shot) or as few as 10 labeled examples per class (10-shot). Design Retrospective benchmarking study. Subjects 4 public datasets (UCSD, IDRiD, REFUGE, ASOCT-MSDC) and 3 private datasets (OHTS, BPEI-DLS, WashU-OCT) of anterior-and posterior-segment ophthalmic imaging. Methods Nine AI models were evaluated across 3 architectural families: MLLMs (Qwen3.8-27B, GLM-5.3-Flash, Gemma-4-31B-it), VFMs (DINOv3, RETFound, VisionFM), and VLMs (CLIP, EyeCLIP, SigLIP2). Models were assessed on disease classification, disease risk and severity grading, anatomical assessment, and lesion localization in fundus and OCT imaging. MLLMs were also compared with a 3D VFM (OCTCube-M) for whole-volume OCT classification. MLLMs were evaluated zero-shot and 10-shot, without additional training. Vision models (VFMs and VLMs) were adapted by linear probing and fine-tuning on the same 10-shot set and on the full training dataset (FD). Main Outcome Measures Disease classification performance (macro-averaged F1, AUROC, quadratic weighted kappa [QWK]), anatomical localization accuracy, and cross-dataset generalization. Results For retinal OCT disease classification, 10-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.94, versus 0.59 (10-shot) and 0.96 (FD) for vision models. For diabetic retinopathy and macular edema grading, 10-shot MLLMs achieved QWKs of 0.69 and 0.73, versus 0.48 and 0.57 (10-shot) and 0.72 and 0.79 (FD) for vision models. For lesion localization, 10-shot MLLMs achieved an F1 of 0.75, versus 0.70 (10-shot) and 0.86 (FD) for vision models. For vertical cup-to-disc ratio estimation (OHTS), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a mean absolute error of 0.14, versus 0.21 (10-shot) for vision models. For whole-volume OCT classification (WashU-OCT), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.71, versus 0.50 (10-shot) and 0.82 (FD) for vision models. Conclusions Open-weight MLLMs given 10 labeled examples per class outperformed VFMs and VLMs trained on the same examples in most tasks and approached the performance of fully trained VFMs and VLMs in selected disease classification and grading tasks. MLLMs also demonstrated promising zero-shot performance on non-public clinical datasets without task-specific training. By reducing the need for large labeled datasets and task-specific model adaptation, MLLMs could broaden who can develop and validate ophthalmic AI.

title: Lesion-Derived Estimated Functional and Structural Connectomes Predict Post-Stroke Recovery Outcomes
abstract: Accurate prognosis after stroke remains challenging, limiting the ability to predict individual recovery. While advanced connectome MRI can provide further prognostically-useful information regarding affected brain networks, its impractical nature has given rise instead to lesion-based estimates of network disruptions. Here, we present a novel pipeline that leverages our recently developed connectome analysis tools to estimate structural disconnection (eSDC) and functional connectivity (eFC) directly from N=96 patient lesion masks for use in predicting motor, language, attention and memory outcomes at multiple timepoints after stroke. Our approach jointly leverages our Network Modification (NeMo) Tool, a database of white matter tractography results that estimates structural disconnectivity (eSDC), and the Krakencoder, a joint autoencoder that estimates functional connectomes (eFC) from the NeMo Tool's output. Models based on eSDC and eFC predicted almost all outcomes, particularly motor outcomes, significantly better than models that used patients' fMRI-based observed FC (oFC) and models based on only lesion information and covariates. Estimated connectome measures also i) retained meaningful inter-individual variability when compared to observed functional connectomes, ii) reflected population-level, stroke-related changes in functional connectomes, and iii) resulted in outcome prediction models with feature importances that aligned with expected networks of relevance to the given outcome. Feature importance analyses also identified distinct predictive signatures across both modality and outcome domain, indicating that eSDC and eFC capture non-redundant, biologically meaningful information about post-stroke network disruption. Together, these findings establish our lesion-based estimates of post-stroke structural and functional connectomes as a practical, information-rich alternative to advanced imaging in patients. This approach allows for probing an individual's affected neural circuitry underlying stroke impairment and recovery, paving the way toward more efficient, accessible, and personalized approaches to post-stroke prognosis and intervention.

title: How Well Does Structural MRI Classify Autism? A Leakage-Free, Site-Aware and Externally Validated Machine-Learning Evaluation in Two ABIDE Cohorts
abstract: Background Many studies report high accuracy for classifying autism spectrum disorder (ASD) from structural MRI, but small samples, single train–test splits, site effects and information leakage can inflate performance. We evaluated how well brain morphometry distinguishes autistic from typically developing (TD) individuals under rigorous, leakage-free validation. Methods FreeSurfer-derived features (n = 280: regional thickness, area and volume; subcortical volumes; Yeo-network composites; asymmetry indices; global measures) from ABIDE II (804 participants; 341 ASD; 12 sites) were used to train logistic regression, linear support vector machine, random forest, XGBoost and multilayer perceptron classifiers. Confound regression (age, age 2 , sex, brain volume), site-wise centring and standardisation were learned within training folds only. Performance was assessed with nested 10-fold cross-validation, leave-one-site-out validation and external validation in ABIDE I (917 participants; 20 sites), and compared with full-pipeline permutation tests and a confound-only baseline. Results Cross-validated discrimination was modest: the best model (regularised logistic regression on all features) reached an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.60 [0.56, 0.64], significantly above chance (permutation p = .002) but far from clinically useful and below a confound-only baseline using age, sex, brain volume and site (AUC 0.63); non-linear models did not perform better (AUC 0.45–0.60 across models and feature sets). Pooled leave-one-site-out AUCs were 0.54–0.61, with large between-site variation, and AUCs in the external ABIDE I cohort were 0.52–0.58. Age-stratified models did not exceed AUC 0.60. Across 300 random 80/20 splits in young adults, test-set AUCs ranged from 0.21 to 0.90, showing that single-split estimates such as 0.74 can arise by chance. Conclusions Under leakage-free, site-aware and externally validated evaluation, structural MRI morphometry classifies autism only slightly better than chance. Reports of high accuracy should be interpreted with caution, and the heterogeneity of autism argues for stratification and normative approaches rather than binary diagnostic classifiers.

title: Strategies of mechanical adaptations of circulating tumor cells and properties of their cellular microenvironment have predictive and prognostic biomarker value
abstract: Mechanically demanding conditions in the blood circulation damage and kill majority of tumor-shed circulating tumor cells (CTCs). Mechanical fitness: a set of mechanical properties detected with atomic force spectroscopy based force spectrometry supports survival of CTCs. We propose that live CTCs isolated from peripheral blood of prostate cancer patients represent distinct strategies of fitness promoting mechanical adaptations to the fluid shear stress. Some of the cells mimicked properties of erythrocytes (high stiffness) or leukocytes (high deformability). The clustering strategy characterized by exceptionally high adhesion is ingenious to CTCs and not found in blood cells. The abundance of CTCs with elevated adhesion has a predictive value for prostate cancer patients starting 1 st round of androgen deprivation therapy. Moreover, a “high adhesion score” based on individual cells’ or average patient-specific adhesion is instrumental to stratify recurrent patients that underwent diagnostic imaging by PSMA-PET/CT and clarify inconclusive PSMA scan results. Including contribution of erythrocyte-like strategy broadened the predictive power of CTC mechanophenotyping. Improved biomarking opportunities to predict early castration resistances were noted when the composition of CTC microenvironment was included alongside the mechanical properties. We demonstrated previously that the CTC microenvironment is formed by large cells co-purifying by microfiltration of the blood of cancer patients. Analysis of the association of particular components of CTC microenvironment with the clustering strategy led to pointing at highly adhesive CTC-EMT. However, in the advanced patients adhesiveness of CTC-EMT was surpassed by tumor hybrid cells (THCs), a distinctive kind of invasive species formed by incomplete phagocytosis of CTCs by macrophages. THCs changed their mechanical phenotype and strategy preference with disease progression pointing at the dynamic nature of adaptations of tumor-shed cells to circulation conditions.

title: 2D U-NET Deep Learning Architecture for Atherosclerotic Lesion Segmentation and Quantification
abstract: Mice are commonly used for experimental atherosclerosis research, and a common procedure involves morphometric analysis of atherosclerotic lesions on Oil Red O-stained cross-sections of the aortic root. However, manual measurement of atherosclerotic lesion sizes on numerous histological sections is tedious and time-consuming. Here, we developed a deep learning model based on convolutional neural network to quantify atherosclerotic lesions in cross-sectioned aortic roots of mice. Microscopy images were taken from cross-sectioned aortic roots of genetically diverse F2 mice derived from BALB/cJ and LP/J Apoe knockout mice and fed 12 weeks of a Western diet. Aortic cross-sections were stained with Oil Red O and hematoxylin and images captured. Atherosclerotic lesions were manually segmented in 2553 images using Zeiss AxioVision. These images were split into 1,533 for training the U-NET model, 510 for validation, and 510 images for testing. The developed model was evaluated for its performance to measure atherosclerotic lesions by comparing with manual measurement in test images. The model achieved a high degree of accuracy, with an Fl score of 0.82, a Jaccard score of 0.72, a Recall of 0.80, a precision of 0.87, and a correlation coefficient value of 0.98. While manual lesion measurement took approximately 5 minutes per image, the model performed the task in ~3.35 seconds, reducing measurement time by 98.9%. The developed 2D U-NET model provides a new platform for rapid and accurate quantification of atherosclerotic lesion sizes on Oil Red O-stained sections.

title: MaxCAT-Net: Hybrid transformer-based skin lesion classification and lightweight segmentation with calibration and cross-dataset validation
abstract: Class imbalance, poor calibration of confidence and poor generalisation under different imaging conditions are restrictions of automated analysis of dermoscopic skin lesions. We propose a hybrid classifier MaxCAT-Net (MaxViT + CBAM + Attention Transformer), which consists of a pre-trained MaxViT-Tiny backbone and the combination of CBAM and two-layer lightweight Transformer encoder and evaluate four encoder-decoder networks for lesion segmentation as a separate task on ISIC 2018 Task 1. All the images of exact/near duplicate were removed and the remaining 10,012 images were distributed lesion-wise (72/14/14) without two or more images having the same type of lesion in HAM10000. On the test set ( n = 1,405), MaxCAT-Net outperformed the baselines of ResNet152-CBAM, MobileNetV3-CBAM, GhostNet-hybrid and single MaxViT-Tiny-CBAM with an accuracy of 0.869 (95% CI 0.847–0.890), balanced accuracy of 0.742, macro-F1 of 0.751 and macro-AUC of 0.944, although ablation gains in macro-F1 (0.017–0.022) were not statistically conclusive. By scaling the temperature, the ECE was decreased from 0.099 to 0.038. In the case of the PAD-UFES-20 dataset, however, the accuracy fell to 0.341 and the melanoma recall rate to 0.096 while for the HAM10000 dataset, the melanoma recall rate was only 0.587. A Swin-T-encoder U-Net was able to achieve a Dice score of 0.903 in segmentation (520 test images), whereas a FasterNet-T0 U-Net (1/10th of the number of parameters) had a Dice score of 0.901 (Holm adjusted p < 0.002), and a standard U-Net had a significantly lower Dice score of 0.888. All results are based on one seed and show trends—not definite improvement.

title: Deep learning grading of Schistosoma japonicum -associated liver fibrosis from ultrasound images: a weighted soft-voting ensemble of convolutional and transformer networks
abstract: Background Schistosomiasis morbidity still persists in China despite extensive progress towards elimination of new and active infections. Diagnosis of liver fibrosis related to Schistosoma japonicum remains challenging due to the subjective nature of ultrasound grading and the shortage of experienced sonographers in endemic counties. Methods We developed a deep learning model that grades schistosomal liver fibrosis from a single B-mode ultrasound image without manual delineation of a region of interest. We used 2,921 images from 2,921 adults (aged 18–88 years, median age 54 years; 46.4% female) from a schistosomiasis hospital in Jiangxi Province, China, between 2019 and 2023. Of these, 12.9%, 34.6%, 32.4% and 20.2% had grade 0, 1, 2 and 3 fibrosis, respectively. Fibrosis grades were based on the clinical ultrasound record and re-evaluation by an experienced radiologist according to the Chinese Hand-book of Schistosomiasis Control; discordant cases were reviewed by a second radiologist and resolved by consensus. Predictions from four neural networks with different architectures (ResNet-18, EfficientNet-B0, DenseNet-121 and Swin-T) were combined by weighted soft voting, with weights derived from validation performance. Results For the four-grade task this model achieved a macro-F1 of 0.8527 (95% CI 0.8184–0.8856), an accuracy of 0.8500 (0.8136–0.8818) and a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.9187 (0.8983–0.9373) on a fixed test set of 440 images. For detecting significant fibrosis (grade 2 or 3; test-set prevalence 0.530), sensitivity was 0.9700, specificity was 0.9179, positive predictive value was 0.9300, negative predictive value was 0.9645, and AUROC was 0.9817. The ensemble achieved a higher macro-F1 than each individual backbone. Every ensemble misclassification was to an adjacent grade; no image with severe fibrosis was classified as no or mild fibrosis, or vice versa, whereas each individual backbone made 1–4 errors spanning two or more grades. Conclusions The model may provide an automated aid for Schistosoma japonicum -associated fibrosis grading and could potentially support screening and follow-up in endemic areas after external validation.

We used 2,921 images from 2,921 adults (aged 18–88 years, median age 54 years; 46.4% female) from a schistosomiasis hospital in Jiangxi Province, China, between 2019 and 2023. Of these, 12.9%, 34.6%, 32.4% and 20.2% had grade 0, 1, 2 and 3 fibrosis, respectively. Fibrosis grades were based on the clinical ultrasound record and re-evaluation by an experienced radiologist according to the Chinese Hand-book of Schistosomiasis Control; discordant cases were reviewed by a second radiologist and resolved by consensus. Predictions from four neural networks with different architectures (ResNet-18, EfficientNet-B0, DenseNet-121 and Swin-T) were combined by weighted soft voting, with weights derived from validation performance.

Results

For the four-grade task this model achieved a macro-F1 of 0.8527 (95% CI 0.8184–0.8856), an accuracy of 0.8500 (0.8136–0.8818) and a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.9187 (0.8983–0.9373) on a fixed test set of 440 images. For detecting significant fibrosis (grade 2 or 3; test-set prevalence 0.530), sensitivity was 0.9700, specificity was 0.9179, positive predictive value was 0.9300, negative predictive value was 0.9645, and AUROC was 0.9817. The ensemble achieved a higher macro-F1 than each individual backbone. Every ensemble misclassification was to an adjacent grade; no image with severe fibrosis was classified as no or mild fibrosis, or vice versa, whereas each individual backbone made 1–4 errors spanning two or more grades.

Conclusions

The model may provide an automated aid for Schistosoma japonicum -associated fibrosis grading and could potentially support screening and follow-up in endemic areas after external validation.

title: Screening for rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease using lung ultrasound: a systematic review and meta-analysis of recent studies
abstract: Interstitial lung diseases (ILD) associated with systemic autoimmune disease can have a strong negative impact on patient outcomes. The diagnostic gold standard is high-resolution computer tomography (HRCT). Numerous studies have proven lung ultrasound's (LUS) utility in ILD, as well as other lung pathologies. Recently, there has been more focus on ILD in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), a previously overlooked complication, and screening methods. The purpose of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to summarize the recent knowledge regarding LUS compared to HRCT in screening ILD in RA patients. We reviewed relevant literature from the last 10 years and selected 12 articles. We included seven of those (totaling 756 patients) in a meta-analysis of diagnostic markers. The pooled sensitivity of LUS was 0.88 (95% CI 0.82-0.92) and pooled specificity was 0.86 (95% CI 0.71-0.94). The pooled LR+ and LR- were found to be 6.63 (95% CI 2.84-15.47) and 0.13 (95% CI 0.08-0.22), respectively. Diagnostic odds ratio was 48.54 (95% CI 13.78-170.98). LUS has high sensitivity and specificity for screening ILD in RA patients across different techniques and scoring systems.

title: ACCURACY OF COMPRESSED SENSING ACCELERATED 3D-FLAIR IN THE DIAGNOSTIC WORK-UP OF MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS AT 1.5 T
abstract: BACKGROUND3D-FLAIR is central to MR-based diagnosis and monitoring of MS, but long acquisition times remain a limitation. OBJECTIVESThis single-center prospective non-inferiority study evaluated whether compressed sensing (CS) - accelerated 3D-FLAIR at 1.5T provides lesion detection comparable to optimized Generalized Autocalibrating Partially Parallel Acquisition (GRAPPA) - accelerated 3D-FLAIR. Optimized CS- and GRAPPA-accelerated 3D-FLAIR sequences were incorporated into MRI examinations in patients with known or suspected MS. The primary endpoint was manual lesion count by two blinded readers using a 10% non-inferiority margin. Secondary endpoints included image quality, SNR, CNR, and automated lesion count and volumetry. RESULTSSixty-eight patients were included (mean age, 40.1{+/-}13.3 years; 61.8% women). CS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR reduced acquisition time by 31.8% compared with GRAPPA (4:00 vs 5:52 minutes). Non-inferiority for manual lesion count was demonstrated for both readers (reader A, p < .0001; reader B, p = .005). Interrater agreement was excellent for CS (ICC = 0.921; 95% CI, 0.837-0.957) and very good for GRAPPA (ICC = 0.851; 95% CI, 0.769-0.906). Subjective image quality was high for both techniques. GRAPPA showed higher objective signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) and contrast-to-noise-ratio (CNR), whereas automated lesion counts and volumes were higher for CS. CONCLUSIONCS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR provided non-inferior lesion detection with substantial scan-time reduction.

title: PROSPECTIVE COMPARISON OF OPTIMIZED COMPRESSED SENSING AND GRAPPA-ACCELERATED 3D-TOF-MRA FOR EVALUATION OF UNTREATED INTRACRANIAL ANEURYSMS AT 1.5 T: A NON-INFERIORITY STUDY
abstract: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES3D-TOF-MRA is a standard non-invasive method for detecting and monitoring intracranial aneurysms, but long scan times remain a limitation. Compressed sensing (CS) acceleration for intracranial aneurysm evaluation has mainly been studied at 3T. This prospective single-center non-inferiority study compared CS-accelerated 3D-TOF at 1.5T with GRAPPA-accelerated 3D-TOF-MRA for evaluating untreated intracranial aneurysms. MATERIALS AND METHODSSample size was determined via a preliminary retrospective study. 25 patients with 32 untreated aneurysms underwent both CS- (factor 7, 3:04 min) and GRAPPA-accelerated (factor 2, 5:00 min) 3D-TOF, yielding a 38.7% scan-time reduction. Two blinded neuroradiologists assessed overall image quality (primary endpoint) and artifacts, subjective CNR, aneurysm delineation and diameters (secondary endpoints). Non-inferiority was tested via one-sided t-test (prespecified 10% margin); interrater agreement used ICC. RESULTSCS demonstrated non-inferiority to GRAPPA for overall image quality in both readers (p [≤] .023), though interrater agreement was low (ICC 0.241-0.262), reflecting subjective variability. Secondary exploratory analyses showed heterogeneous preferences. ROI-based CNR was lower for CS (median 169.6; IQR, 91.0-226. vs. 278.2; 181.0-366.2). Aneurysm diameter measurements showed excellent interrater agreement for both techniques (CS ICC, 0.899-0.980; GRAPPA ICC, 0.877-0.973; all p < .001). CONCLUSIONCS-accelerated 3D-TOF at 1.5T met non-inferiority criteria vs. GRAPPA-TOF for overall image quality, reducing scan time by 38.7% while preserving aneurysm measurement reliability. However, reduced CNR and reader-preference variability important trade-offs. These findings support the use of CS-accelerated-TOF as a time-efficient alternative to GRAPPA-accelerated-TOF in evaluating intracranial aneurysms, though further research on field-strength effects and small aneurysms is warranted.

title: AI-Based MRI Radiomics for Preoperative Detection of Tumor Deposits in Rectal Cancer: A Bivariate Diagnostic Accuracy Meta-analysis
abstract: Background: In rectal cancer (RC), tumor deposits (TDs) are clinically important as they are associated with a negative impact on prognosis and affect risk stratification as well as management plans. MRI radiomics combined with artificial intelligence (AI) has been explored for non-invasive preoperative TDs detection. However, results vary across studies; therefore, we performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to pool their diagnostic test accuracy (DTA). Methods: This systematic review and DTA meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Diagnostic Test Accuracy and reported in adherence to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies (PRISMA-DTA). Databases were screened for DTA studies of MRI-based radiomics predicting TDs in adult RC patients with histopathology as reference. Results: Nine studies (2589 patients) were identified. Across included studies, the bivariate meta-analysis showed pooled sensitivity of 0.765 (95% CI 0.714 - 0.809) and specificity of 0.790 (95% CI 0.750 - 0.825), with overall AUC of 0.845 and very low heterogeneity (I2 = 7.3%). In validation datasets, diagnostic performance remained consistent (AUC 0.806), with pooled sensitivity 0.751 (95% CI 0.681 - 0.809) and specificity 0.751 (95% CI 0.681 - 0.809). For MRI modality, T2 weighted image (T2WI) showed higher sensitivity (0.745) than T2WI plus diffusion weighted image (DWI) (0.697), while T2WI+DWI had higher specificity (0.809 vs 0.737) and AUC (0.829 vs 0.796), with no significant subgroup differences (p[≥]0.192). Models combining radiomics with clinical/radiological variables achieved significantly higher sensitivity (0.842 vs 0.657, p<0.001) and higher AUC (0.827 vs 0.752), with comparable specificity. Conclusion: MRI-based radiomics demonstrates good accuracy for preoperative detection of tumor deposits in RC. The integration of radiomics with clinical or imaging features increases the accuracy of identification. Amongst the MRI modalities, models that utilize the combination of T2WI plus DWI are more accurate than those using T2WI or DWI only.

title: Pathology foundation-model embeddings reveal a morphological landscape of breast lesions beyond diagnostic categories
abstract: Background Despite rapid advances in computational pathology, including foundation-model embeddings, most approaches remain classifier-based. Breast lesion pathology is an area of unmet clinicopathological need and a compelling setting for morphology-based modeling: diagnostic categories occupy overlapping morphological spectra and reflect heterogeneous pathways of tumor development, thereby posing substantial challenges for pathological diagnosis and subsequent clinical decision-making. However, approaches to delineate morphological continua across diagnostic categories and tumor development remain understudied. Here, we leveraged morphology-based foundation-model embeddings to define a morphologic state space across breast lesion categories and dissect how these embeddings could reflect a pathobiological continuum or sequence associated with tumor development. Methods To model breast lesion categories in continuous morphology space, we established a leakage-controlled, patient-aware workflow using the frozen foundation model Prov-GigaPath and the BReAst Carcinoma Subtyping (BRACS) dataset, a pathologist-annotated hematoxylin-and-eosin (H&E) breast lesion dataset spanning normal tissue, benign proliferative lesions, atypical lesions, ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and invasive carcinoma (IC). Using the BRACS training split, we defined a train-derived principal component analysis (PCA) morphology space. We then performed two complementary analyses: normal-rooted k-nearest-neighbor (kNN)-Dijkstra graph-distance scoring to derive a trajectory-like morphology score without imposing the full ordinal diagnostic sequence; pairwise Energy distance and squared maximum mean discrepancy with a radial-basis-function kernel (RBF-MMD²) to quantify order-free distributional separation among diagnostic categories. Validation and test data were projected into the train-defined reference space to assess reproducibility. Results Prov-GigaPath embeddings defined a train-derived morphology space with category-associated organization. Without imposing the full diagnostic sequence, normal-rooted kNN-Dijkstra graph distances recovered a trajectory-like morphology arrangement from normal/benign to malignant lesions. Order-free Energy distance and RBF-MMD² further supported graded separation among lesion categories. Validation and test datasets preserved the pathological organization. Furthermore, morphological embeddings dissected DCIS heterogeneity associated with concurrent invasive carcinoma, without requiring additional molecular information. Conclusions Leveraging morphology-based foundation-model embeddings, we defined a morphologic state space across breast lesion categories, allowing nuanced positioning of breast lesions along a pathobiological continuum associated with tumor development. Our approaches pave the way for extracting biologically and clinically relevant information from routine histopathology to guide molecular testing, individualized risk assessment, and cost-efficient clinicopathological decision-making. Highlights Overlapping morphological features challenge breast diagnostic categorization Foundation-model embeddings defined a morphologic state space Embeddings allow nuanced positioning along morphological continua across categories Embeddings dissected DCIS heterogeneity associated with concurrent invasive carcinoma Latent morphological signals in H&E slides may refine individualized risk assessment

title: Interpretable Machine Learning Links Group-Specific Plasma Proteomics to Regional Structural Neuroimaging in Alzheimer’s Disease
abstract: Background Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathology begins years before clinical symptoms, highlighting the need for scalable biomarkers that capture biological changes across the AD continuum. Broader plasma proteomics may capture systemic processes that vary with disease stage, yet their relationship to AD-related brain neurodegeneration remains unclear. We aimed to identify plasma proteomic signatures across cognitively normal (CN), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and AD and evaluate their neuroanatomical associations. Methods We analyzed 146 plasma analytes from 565 Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) participants (58 CN, 396 MCI, 111 AD). Group-specific proteomic signatures were identified using pairwise classification models with nested 5×5 cross-validation. SHAP quantified feature importance, with the top 15 proteins per comparison being prioritized for MRI association analysis. We analyzed 103 regional structural MRI volumes harmonized across 57 acquisition sites using ComBat. Separate ordinary least squares regression tested protein-MRI associations, adjusting for age, sex, APOE ε4, diagnosis, and intracranial volume, followed by Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Results Classification models using proteomic data achieved AUC of 0.956 ± 0.017 for CN vs MCI, 0.963 ± 0.011 for MCI vs. AD, and 0.836 ± 0.085 for CN vs. AD. SHAP identified group-dependent proteomic signatures. No protein-MRI associations survived FDR correction for CN vs. MCI. In MCI vs. AD, higher cortisol was associated with lower left precuneus and superior parietal volumes, while higher osteopontin was associated with lower left paracentral and accumbens volumes. In CN vs. AD, higher vitronectin was associated with lower posterior corpus callosum volume. Conclusion These findings suggest that plasma proteomics capture group-specific systemic biological signals across the AD continuum. Linking ML-prioritized plasma proteins to regional brain structure provides neuroanatomical context for blood-based biomarker discovery.

title: Bundlemorphometry: Spatially Resolved White Matter Bundle Shape Analysis Using Nonlinear Streamline-Based Registration
abstract: ABSTRACT Diffusion MRI tractometry quantifies microstructural properties along white matter (WM) bundles but does not directly measure their geometry, potentially overlooking localized morphological alterations. Here, we introduce BundleMorphometry, a framework for quantifying local WM bundle shape using the analytical Jacobian of nonlinear streamline-based registration. Individual subject bundles are registered to a reference atlas bundle using BundleWarp, a streamline-based nonlinear registration method. We derive the analytical Jacobian of the resulting deformation field and compute its log-determinant (log det J) to quantify local expansion and compression at each streamline point. To enable spatially resolved group comparisons, these measurements are projected onto the two-dimensional grid, capturing variations along and across each bundle. We evaluated BundleMorphometry using two clinical datasets comprising patients with glioma and Parkinson’s disease (PD). In the glioma dataset, BundleMor-phometry revealed spatially extensive deformation patterns in lesion-affected WM bundles that were not captured by displacement magnitude alone. Additionally, in a group analysis of the PD dataset (32 patients and 32 healthy controls), we identified significant localized morphological differences in the corpus callosum forceps major, mid-body and right spinothalamic tract, with distinct patterns of expansion and compression. These findings demonstrate the potential of BundleMorphometry to advance conventional tractometry by enabling spatially resolved analysis of bundle morphology.

title: Generalizable virtual staining from histopathology to spatial proteomics across biological scales
abstract: Large histology archives capture morphological correlates of molecular tissue states but lack direct spatial protein measurements. In this study, we show that routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histology can provide a queryable, morphology-based representation of spatial protein expression that remains informative from pixels to patients. To achieve this, we developed QUEST, a model framework that represents protein markers as semantic queries for flexible multiplex immunofluorescence (MIF) prediction. Trained on a heterogeneous atlas of paired H&E and MIF images comprising over 10,000 tissue regions, QUEST captured morphological patterns associated with protein markers and reconstructed their expression intensities across diverse tissue types and cohorts. Its utility extended beyond image reconstruction and preserved biologically meaningful information across multiple scales: virtual staining preserved protein marker expression at the cellular and tissue scales, supported cell phenotyping, cellular neighborhood analysis, and characterization of spatial tissue organization, retained clinically relevant signals for patient stratification, and enabled H&E-based queries to retrieve MIF references with similar molecular profiles. These findings position virtual staining not simply as image generation but as a flexible interface between routine histology and spatial proteomics, expanding the analytical value of existing H&E archives.

title: RyR2-Mediated Ca 2+ Leak Drives Progressive Arrhythmogenic Cardiomyopathy
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Abnormal sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca 2+ release through ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2) is a well-established mechanism of ventricular arrhythmias. Whether persistent RyR2 dysfunction can also initiate the structural remodeling characteristic of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM) remains unknown. We tested the hypothesis that chronic RyR2-mediated Ca 2+ leak is sufficient to couple electrical instability to progressive cardiomyopathy. Methods We generated a rabbit carrying the severe gain-of-function RyR2-V2475F mutation and characterized disease progression using longitudinal cardiac phenotyping, continuous electrocardiographic monitoring, cellular electrophysiology and Ca 2+ imaging, histopathology, biochemical analyses, and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq). Therapeutic potential was evaluated by continuous treatment with the selective RyR2 inhibitor ent -verticilide for two months. Results RyR2-V2475F rabbits developed spontaneous ventricular tachyarrhythmias, sudden cardiac death, and progressive right ventricular (RV)-dominant fibrofatty cardiomyopathy recapitulating major features of human ACM. Malignant ventricular arrhythmias preceded overt structural remodeling and were associated at the cellular level with early spontaneous Ca 2+ release and early afterdepolarizations. Early disease was characterized by remodeling of excitation-contraction coupling with preserved SR Ca 2+ load and contractile function despite RyR2 dysfunction; upon disease progression, these compensatory changes were accompanied by SR Ca 2+ depletion, impaired RV contractility and reduced left ventricular filling. Single-nucleus transcriptomics identified early fibroblast expansion and predicted cardiomyocyte-centered paracrine signaling before advanced fibrofatty infiltration. Cardiomyocytes also exhibited an altered lipid-metabolic transcriptome and intracellular lipid accumulation, accompanied by enhanced mitochondrial Ca 2+ uptake. Selective RyR2 inhibition markedly reduced ventricular tachycardia burden and preserved RV contraction and LV filling during disease progression. Conclusions Severe RyR2 gain-of-function can lead to both malignant ventricular arrhythmias and progressive arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy in a large-animal model, establishing persistent intracellular Ca 2+ dysregulation as a mechanistic link between electrical and structural heart disease. The ability of selective RyR2 inhibition to suppress arrhythmias and preserve cardiac function identifies RyR2 as a potentially actionable therapeutic target in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

title: Peripheral immune biomarkers, brain imaging phenotypes and treatment response in major depressive disorder
abstract: Immune dysregulation is implicated in major depressive disorder (MDD), but its links to clinical features and in vivo brain phenotypes remain uncertain. We examined ten plasma biomarkers in 36 unmedicated MDD patients and 48 control participants using high-sensitivity immune profiling at baseline, alongside PET/MR imaging of brain serotonin transporter (SERT) binding and regional structural measures. Patients underwent three months of antidepressant treatment and were followed up with MR imaging. Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) was higher in MDD patients (β = 0.66, 95% CI 0.22 - 1.11), and interleukin-33 (IL-33) correlated with subcortical volumes across all participants (β = 0.22, 95% CI 0.07 - 0.38). No marker correlated with SERT binding or cortical thickness after correction, and neither SERT binding nor brain structural measures differed by diagnosis. In the longitudinal analysis, interleukin-13 (IL-13) was associated with greater antidepressant response during first-line treatment with escitalopram (β = 1.09, 95% CI 0.56 - 1.61). IL-15 and IL-13 showed nominal associations with hippocampal volume increase after treatment. These findings support astroglial involvement in MDD and link peripheral immune variation to subcortical brain structure. IL-13 is a candidate prognostic marker of response to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Its tentative association with longitudinal changes in hippocampal volume suggests that immune processes in MDD may be related to both the capacity for clinical improvement and brain structural plasticity during treatment.

title: Investigating AI's potential in risk-stratifying lung cancer screenings for extending screening intervals and reducing workload: A retrospective analysis of a tertiary hospital cohort
abstract: ObjectiveWe aimed to 1) evaluate whether AI algorithms could identify a very low-risk sub-population Lung-RADS 1/2 cases suitable for a safe switch to biennial screening, and 2) externally validate Sybil, an imaging-based deep learning lung cancer risk prediction tool. Materials and methodsWe gathered all lung cancer screenings (LCSs) from a tertiary safety-net hospital (n=3120, up to September 2024), manually extracted relevant clinical data, and analyzed Sybils performance across various subgroups, with a specific focus on Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases. We simulated LCS interval extension using Sybil and the Brock model risk scores calibrated on a subset of the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST). Confidence intervals were obtained through bootstrapping. ResultsThe median follow-up was 2.3 years (interquartile range 1.5-3.1), with a total 6-year cancer incidence rate of 2.3% (72/3120). Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases comprised 90.5% of our scans. Sybils overall area under the curve (AUC) ranged from 0.819 to 0.912; while its 2-year AUC for Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases was 0.746. In the screening interval extension simulation, calibrating for a 30% shift to biennial screening translated into 33.8% of negative screens in our data being safely extended using Sybil, with no delayed cancers. The Brock model demonstrated an AUC of 0.513 on our data, with a sensitivity of 18.2% using the 1.5% threshold. ConclusionSybil has the potential to safely extend LCS intervals for low-risk individuals, reducing radiology workload and opening spots for life-saving new screenings. Key pointsO_LIWe investigated whether AI risk stratification tools could identify the lowest-risk individuals undergoing lung cancer screening suitable for switching to a biennial screening schedule. C_LIO_LIIn our simulations, Sybil reduced follow-up screening load by at least 30% through switching the lowest-risk Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases to biennial screening without delayed cancer diagnoses. C_LIO_LIVery low-risk individuals, as predicted by AI algorithms, could potentially be placed on biennial screening schedules, reducing radiology department workload and freeing time for new patients. title: Olfactory Function in Preclinical Alzheimer’s Disease: A Multi-Cohort Study
abstract: Introduction Olfactory impairment is an early feature of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). However, it is unclear if olfactory performance reflects early pathological changes during preclinical AD and/or predicts subsequent clinical progression among characterized cognitively normal (CN) individuals. We aimed to determine whether odor identification differs by amyloid status, relates to medial temporal lobe (MTL) tau burden and morphometry, and predicts longitudinal conversion to mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Methods We analyzed data from 257 cognitively normal (CN) older adults enrolled in PREVENT-AD (n = 217) and UCLouvain (n = 40), including 76 amyloid-positive (CN A+) and 181 amyloid-negative participants (CN A–). Participants completed olfactory testing, underwent tau-PET imaging, and structural MRI. Results CN A+ participants had significantly lower odor identification performance than CN A− participants, with no evidence of cohort heterogeneity. Tau-PET associations with odor identification differed by cohort. After whole-brain FDR correction and exclusion of extreme values, parahippocampal tau burden was negatively associated with odor identification score in UCLouvain ([18F]MK-6240), an association that was not found in PREVENT-AD ([ 18 F]flortaucipir). No morphometric association survived multiple comparison correction. In 250 participants with longitudinal follow-up, each 10-percentage-point higher odor identification score was associated with a 16% lower hazard of incident MCI, independent of baseline global cognition and APOE ε4-carrier status. Discussion Odor identification was lower in preclinical AD and associated with incident MCI independently of baseline global cognition and APOE ε4-carrier status. Its association with parahippocampal tau burden differed between cohorts, supporting further investigation using harmonized imaging methods. Clinical trial registration Not applicable; this was an observational cohort study.

title: Rapid Detection and Initial Treatment of Life-Threatening Subdural Hematoma in a Sheep Model
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is the leading cause of death and disability in people under 40 worldwide. There is an unmet need for detection and treatment of life-threatening TBI when computed tomography (CT) scanners and neurosurgeons are unavailable. We developed a new handheld frequency-domain multidetector infrared hemorrhage detection device. Using the new device, military pre-hospital medics required <4 minutes to detect life-threatening subdural hematoma in a sheep model. We developed a second device that allows non-neurosurgeons to safely create a burr hole and partially remove clotted subdural blood. In sheep, the treatment device reduced intracranial pressure within 20 minutes, and improved post-anesthesia blinded neurological outcomes. With human use adaptation, these devices could allow rapid detection and initial treatment of some life-threatening TBIs in challenging situations.

title: Late radiation-induced brain injury is associated with functional cerebrovascular impairment without structural vessel loss in mice
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Radiation-induced brain injury (RIBI) is a major and often irreversible complication of cranial radiotherapy, affecting up to 90% of long-term survivors. Although cerebrovascular damage is a leading mechanistic hypothesis, whether chronic resting hypoperfusion occurs independently of structural vessel loss remains unknown. The aim of this study was to comprehensively characterize cerebrovascular, structural, and behavioral outcomes in a murine model of late RIBI to determine the primary drivers of vascular dysfunction. Methods Adult C57BL/6 mice underwent 12 Gy whole-brain irradiation and were assessed one year later using laser speckle contrast imaging (LSCI), 7T MRI, immunohistochemistry, and behavioral testing. Results Irradiated mice exhibited reduced pial flow velocity and flow area by LSCI, indicative of upstream cerebrovascular dysfunction, while bulk cortical tissue perfusion was preserved. This pial hypoperfusion was accompanied by cerebral atrophy, decreased T2* relaxation time and tissue iron deposition consistent with chronic microhemorrhage across multiple brain regions by MRI, blood-brain barrier disruption reflected by reduced ZO-1 and VE-cadherin expression, and increased anxiety-like behavior. Strikingly, capillary density, pericyte coverage, astrocyte endfeet, and NeuN-positive neuronal nuclei were all preserved. Conclusion These findings demonstrate that functional vascular impairment - not structural vessel or neuronal loss - drives hypoperfusion and blood-brain barrier disruption in late RIBI. This dissociation between vascular dysfunction and rarefaction reframes the pathophysiology of RIBI and identifies endothelial dysfunction as a tractable therapeutic target for intervention.

Background

Radiation-induced brain injury (RIBI) is a major and often irreversible complication of cranial radiotherapy, affecting up to 90% of long-term survivors. Adult C57BL/6 mice underwent 12 Gy whole-brain irradiation and were assessed one year later using laser speckle contrast imaging (LSCI), 7T MRI, immunohistochemistry, and behavioral testing.

Results

Irradiated mice exhibited reduced pial flow velocity and flow area by LSCI, indicative of upstream cerebrovascular dysfunction, while bulk cortical tissue perfusion was preserved. This pial hypoperfusion was accompanied by cerebral atrophy, decreased T2* relaxation time and tissue iron deposition consistent with chronic microhemorrhage across multiple brain regions by MRI, blood-brain barrier disruption reflected by reduced ZO-1 and VE-cadherin expression, and increased anxiety-like behavior. These findings demonstrate that functional vascular impairment - not structural vessel or neuronal loss - drives hypoperfusion and blood-brain barrier disruption in late RIBI. This dissociation between vascular dysfunction and rarefaction reframes the pathophysiology of RIBI and identifies endothelial dysfunction as a tractable therapeutic target for intervention.

title: Cortical Thinning in Adults with Prader–Willi Syndrome: Distribution Across Functional Networks and Associations with BMI and the GH/IGF-1 Axis
abstract: Prader–Willi syndrome (PWS) is a rare neurogenetic disorder associated with neuropsychiatric, metabolic, endocrine, and physical abnormalities. Although previous neuroimaging studies have identified regional gray matter alterations, cortical thickness (CT) abnormalities and their distribution across large-scale functional brain networks remain poorly characterized in adults with PWS. We investigated cortical morphology in 23 adults with PWS and 22 age- and sex-matched healthy controls who underwent structural MRI. Cortical reconstruction and surface-based morphometric analyses were performed using FreeSurfer. Between-group differences in CT were assessed using age, sex, and intracranial volume as covariates. Associations between CT and clinical, cognitive, anthropometric, and endocrine measures were examined using Spearman correlations. Significant cortical regions were further mapped onto an a priori functional network atlas. Adults with PWS showed reduced CT in a left-hemispheric cluster involving the inferior precentral gyrus, insula, inferior temporal cortex, and orbitofrontal cortex. This cluster overlapped predominantly with the somatomotor, auditory, cingulo-opercular, language, and frontoparietal networks. Within the PWS group, lower CT was associated with higher body mass index and poorer global functioning. CT was positively associated with IGF-1 levels and was greater in participants with a history of growth hormone therapy during childhood. These findings indicate cortical thinning across regions belonging to multiple functional networks involved in sensorimotor, attentional, language, and executive processes, extending previous volumetric findings. The associations with body mass index, functional measures, and the GH/IGF-1 axis suggest that cortical morphology may reflect an interplay between genetic vulnerability and potentially modifiable metabolic and endocrine factors, raising the possibility of a neuroprotective role for GH/IGF-1 signaling.

title: Statistical design of Path to Prevention platform trial in early neuronal alpha-synuclein disease
abstract: The Path to Prevention (P2P) platform trial is a first-in-class, phase 2A, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled learning study. Its design expedites the assessment of investigational therapies for the treatment of early-stage Neuronal α-Synuclein Disease (NSD), a biological disease continuum that encompasses and often precedes clinically manifest Parkinson’s Disease. P2P is embedded within the Parkinson’s Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI), a robust observational longitudinal cohort study on Parkinson’s disease progression and a trial-facilitating enrollment framework. A regimen , comprised of an active investigational therapy and a matched placebo control, evaluates a therapeutic candidate within the P2P perpetual platform framework. Multiple regimens can be enrolled, enabling efficient testing of multiple therapeutics. A two-stage randomization scheme determines regimen sample size with 125 participants assigned to a regimen’s active therapy and a variable number to placebo control. The treated follow up period is a minimum of 96 weeks and a maximum of 144 weeks, with the last randomized participant followed for 96 weeks. As a pioneering interventional trial in early-stage NSD, P2P endpoint selection was critically informed by modeling and analysis of available PPMI data. In P2P, regimens will be evaluated for efficacy using two primary endpoints: 1) a biomarker outcome of Dopamine Transporter Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography (DAT SPECT) imaging measured by the bilateral putamen Specific Binding Ratio (SBR) and 2) a clinical outcome measured by the Movement Disorder Society-Sponsored Revision of the Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) Part III score. Each endpoint will be assessed separately using a longitudinal Bayesian mixed effects model, which compares the active treatment group to the shared placebo control group. The model uses regimen-specific controls at full weight and dynamically discounts controls from other regimens. Additionally, placebo control estimates are supplemented by non-randomized control data from the PPMI cohort. Clinical trial simulations, informed by longitudinal data from 275 P2P-eligible PPMI study participants (Age 60-81, 35% Female, 65% Male), were conducted to evaluate the design. Each regimen is well-powered to detect a 40% slowing in progression for both the clinical and biomarker primary endpoints when comparing active treatment to randomized control data. Supplementing the control estimation with non-randomized, P2P-eligible registry participant data increases power in the explored scenarios up to 4% for each endpoint. The embedded P2P platform trial is a powerful learning study that leverages statistical efficiencies from the platform trial design and established PPMI infrastructure and is poised to advance treatment development in early-stage NSD.

title: Personalized Prediction of Differences in fMRI Connectivity Estimates Across Preprocessing Pipelines
abstract: Longitudinal functional MRI of the human brain is valuable for tracking changes in functional connectivity (FC) associated with disease progression or treatment response. Even so, measured FC values depend on preprocessing, and nuisance regression and temporal filtering affect individuals differently. We examined whether we could use earlier scans to predict how preprocessing would affect a later scan. In 69 ADNI (Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative) participants scanned three times, we measured how nuisance regression and filtering, alone and in sequence, changed the measured FC. A ridge regression model combined these responses with baseline FC from the third scan to predict the effect of reversing the processing order. Just four coefficients were shared across 79,800 connections. In leave-one-participant-out testing, mean squared error was 0.012, compared with 0.017 for predicting the same average response for everyone. It outperformed the best of seven alternative predictions chosen for each participant (0.013; normalized gain 0.069, 95% bootstrap interval 0.006–0.134), with lower error in 44 of 69 participants. About half the benefit of using each person’s earlier responses, rather than the average across participants, came from which connections changed. This advantage persisted after accounting for acquisition variables. The ADNI-trained model reduced mean error in ten Midnight Scan Club participants without refitting. These results support using personal preprocessing history to predict changes in connectivity estimates on newly acquired scans.
